speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Progressive Conservative Party Deputy House Leader
subsubtopic: PROPOSED DELAY IN IMPLEMENTATION OF RAIL PASSENGER POLICY-MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise under the provisions of Standing Order 43 on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity. In view of the commitment by the former minister of transport to allow the Standing Committee on Transport and Communications the full opportunity of examining transportation policy in Canada as a total concept, and in view of the statement by the present minister of his intention to continue this full investigation, and in view of the desirability of attaining a reasonable and co-ordinated transportation policy to extricate the country from the present mess, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Capilano (Mr. Huntington):
That this House direct the Minister of Transport to withhold implementation of rail passenger policy until the government announces a full and co-ordinate policy for transportation rather than piecemeal announcements respecting individual modes of transportation.

speechtext:

subsubtopic: POSSIBLE MEASURES TO AVERT STRIKE OF RAILWAY EMPLOYEES-ROLE OF ANTI-INFLATION BOARD
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before I put my question may I express the hope that while the Prime Minister might think out loud I hope the government whip does not start thinking out loud.
My question is for the Minister of Labour and is in connection with the expected breakdown of negotiations for a new collective agreement between the railways and significant railway unions. Can the Minister of Labour indicate to the House whether he proposes to take any measure to head off a possible railway strike?

speakeroldname: Hon. John C. Munro (Minister of Labour):
subsubtopic: POSSIBLE MEASURES TO AVERT STRIKE OF RAILWAY EMPLOYEES-ROLE OF ANTI-INFLATION BOARD
speechtext: Yes, Mr. Speaker. Of course, the Leader of the Opposition will be aware that under the Act I am required within 15 days of receiving notice of a breakdown from the union, which I officially received last Thursday, to appoint a commissioner to inject himself in an endeavour to mediate a settlement. I am considering that course of action today, tomorrow and the next few days.

subsubtopic: POSSIBLE MEASURES TO AVERT STRIKE OF RAILWAY EMPLOYEES-ROLE OF ANTI-INFLATION BOARD
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, what would be the parameters within which such a mediator would work with regard to the increase in wages. Have the parameters been determined by the Anti-Inflation Board or will such a commissioner work in the dark as to what would be acceptable to the Anti-Inflation Board?

subsubtopic: POSSIBLE MEASURES TO AVERT STRIKE OF RAILWAY EMPLOYEES-ROLE OF ANTI-INFLATION BOARD
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I should make it quite clear that I am talking here about a single man commissioner as opposed to another possibility that of the appointment of a board of conciliation. But generally speaking, I would suppose that if any mediator were successful in bringing the parties together and in arriving at a collective agreement, which I would hope be the case here, that collective agreement might be subject to interpretation by the Anti-Inflation Board just like all other collective agreements which fall under the policy.

subsubtopic: POSSIBLE MEASURES TO AVERT STRIKE OF RAILWAY EMPLOYEES-ROLE OF ANTI-INFLATION BOARD
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, does it seem sensible to the minister that he would ask for the commissioner or mediator to take on a task without precise terms of reference, without the mediator knowing what the terms of reference really are and possibly bringing the parties together on a basis that is quite unacceptable to the Anti-Inflation Board? Would it not seem to the minister to make far more sense to get the Anti-Inflation Board to lay down the parameters in advance rather than take the company through a fruitless and possibly quite disastrous exercise?

subsubtopic: POSSIBLE MEASURES TO AVERT STRIKE OF RAILWAY EMPLOYEES-ROLE OF ANTI-INFLATION BOARD
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I think it is quite clear that the proper procedure under the legislation and the regulations backing up that legislation is that either one of the parties or both parties can approach, if they wish, the Anti-Inflation Board for advice on a proposed or mutual agreement, and it is possible that one of the parties might do that following which they would arrive at some type of agreement.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on Friday the right hon. member for Prince Albert asked me a question concerning a letter sent by the Clerk of the Privy Council to the deputy minister of justice with regard to the seat of government. I have now had an opportunity to look into this matter and wish to inform the House that the Clerk of the Privy Council did indeed write to the deputy minister of justice in the course of preparations for the reference to a joint parliamentary committee of matters relating to the national capital. The
Oral Questions
purpose of this letter was to determine the full implications of a recommendation made to the government by Mr. Douglas Fullerton in his report on a special study on the national capital.
Hon. members will recall that the first recommendation contained in this report, which was made public on November 1, 1974, was that the federal government-and I quote:
Accept the National Capital Region as its 'seat of government' and as its capital.
The government had not decided at that time, did not decide later and has not decided now to accept this recommendation. It awaits the report of the joint parliamentary committee to which this House and the Senate referred the Fullerton report.
In these circumstances, Mr. Speaker, you will understand that it is difficult to believe that we had any hidden design to circumvent parliament or, indeed, the Canadian public. Parliament is being consulted and will continue to be consulted. May I just-

subsubtopic: CHANGING NAME OF OTTAWA-GOVERNMENT INTENTIONS WITH REGARD TO NON-STATUTORY PROCEDURE
speechtext: Oh, oh!

subsubtopic: CHANGING NAME OF OTTAWA-GOVERNMENT INTENTIONS WITH REGARD TO NON-STATUTORY PROCEDURE
speechtext: Let him answer the question.

subsubtopic: CHANGING NAME OF OTTAWA-GOVERNMENT INTENTIONS WITH REGARD TO NON-STATUTORY PROCEDURE
speechtext: You should do it on motions, Mitch.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subsubtopic: CHANGING NAME OF OTTAWA-GOVERNMENT INTENTIONS WITH REGARD TO NON-STATUTORY PROCEDURE
speechtext:
Order, please. We are facing, in this exercise, the balance of the difficulty referred to many times by members of the House concerning a minister who has given an undertaking. The Chair has reacted by refusing supplementaries with respect to undertakings given by ministers who said they would investigate matters and come back with an answer at a later date. The complaint has often been that the minister has not come back at a later date. Frankly, we faced this difficulty originally when we did not introduce into the new process procedures to that effect. This is taking place now. Desirable though that may be, there are two shortcomings in this process.
First, I would not want the minister to be given the privilege of going on too long. Second, of course, someone ought to be permitted to ask supplementary questions on the matter; indeed, the original questioner is not now present in the House. I do not know whether someone would want to take on that responsibility for him, or whether the information ought simply to be on record, awaiting the presence in the House of the right hon. gentleman who put the question originally, with the understanding that there would be supplementaries at that time.

subsubtopic: CHANGING NAME OF OTTAWA-GOVERNMENT INTENTIONS WITH REGARD TO NON-STATUTORY PROCEDURE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not object to the minister giving a succinct response, but he has gone away beyond that. I rise again, not to suggest how Mr. Speaker should conduct the House, but to say that I hope this procedure will not constitute a precedent and that anybody who does this in future will be succinct, factual and not spend a long time answering.

Mr. Speaker, I rise on a point of order regarding the business of the House today, with particular reference to the procedure of taking questions as notice which has become more prevalent in the last few weeks. Our question period was never designed to handle replies to questions asked on another day. I would ask Your Honour to give consideration to referring this matter to the Standing Committee on Procedure and Organization so that consideration could be given to having these answers presented during a later question period with or without the right of further limited questioning on the answer. Some consideration could be given to having such answers provided at another time slot during the question period, perhaps immediately following it.

If questions are to be taken as notice, with replies provided at a later time, this will create a continuing problem during our question periods. I would, therefore, ask Your Honour to give some consideration to the referral of this matter to the appropriate committee so that almost immediate consideration can be given in order to eliminate the difficulty which is obviously going to become a continuous one.

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Progressive Conservative Party Deputy House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on the same point of order. In the matter raised by the hon. member who just spoke there is a question worthy of consideration by the committee. There is another problem which arises during the question period. Many ministers quite honestly say in answer to questions that they do not have the specific information but will inform the hon. member. This reply usually takes the form of a letter from the minister's office to the hon. member. The questions are asked as public matters on the floor of the House and then become private matters between the ministry and the hon. member, with little opportunity for the answer to become public. I would think that in addition to the matter raised by the hon. member for Timiskaming this question might also be referred to the committee.
If some way were found of making these answers public, I think this would make the question period much more meaningful and, though I hesitate to say it, it might be a way of perhaps having ministers a little better informed in terms of answering questions which are asked about urgent public matters.

I was urged by the media to appear on all sorts of programs to give the reply I had promised the right hon. member for Prince Albert. I resisted that temptation because I thought it was only appropriate that I should give the answer here in the House of Commons. When I tried to give the answer there was objection because the right hon. member for Prince Albert was not present. So there is a real problem. I hope it is one to which we can address our minds.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO LIMIT ANNUAL INCREASE IN PER CAPITA COST OF INSURED SERVICES UNDER MEDICAL CARE PLANS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, Bill C-68 seeks to amend the Medical Care Act so as to limit the federal government's contribution to any increase in the cost of medicare above specified limits. When taken in conjunction with the notices given the
Medical Care
provinces last June announcing the federal government's intention to terminate the present five-year agreement with regard to hospital insurance, this legislation represents the beginning of the federal government's opting out of the solemn undertakings given the provinces when the hospital insurance and medicare program was introduced. The provincial governments were induced to participate in these worth-while programs on the assurance that Ottawa would pay approximately 50 per cent of the cost.
We are now witnessing a betrayal of these commitments and a determination to shift the burden to the provinces, with what I predict will be disastrous results. This is legislation which ought to be resisted by every member who wants to protect our present health care programs and who wants to promote better relations between the federal government and the provincial governments of this country.
Last Wednesday, the minister opened his statement with the declaration that "Canadians enjoy one of the best health systems in the world." It is true that we have made commendable progress in this field in the last 20 years, but >ve should not delude ourselves that our system is the best in the world. Many countries, such as the Scandinavian countries, the United Kingdom, Holland, New Zealand, West Germany and Israel have had comprehensive health insurance programs for a much longer period and which cover a much wider range of health services than we have. So far, our health programs have covered only hospital and medical services insofar as federal financing is concerned. Such additional services as home nursing, denticare, prosthetic appliances and pharmacare have been financed entirely by some of the provinces at a cost for all the provinces of $1.5 billion this fiscal year and an estimated cost of $1.9 billion in the coming fiscal year, plus a supplemental payment of another $800 million annually until 1980.
Those provinces which cannot afford these additional services have had to deny these benefits to their people because Ottawa has failed to expand the medical care program beyond the services provided for in 1968. Now the federal government wants to limit its financial contribution even in respect of the present limited programs. The fact is, of course, that the Liberal party always has been a reluctant proponent of comprehensive health insurance. Let me review briefly the history of health insurance in this country and the part the Liberal party has played in that program. In 1919 the Liberal convention held in Ottawa pledged itself to institute a comprehensive health insurance program. If my recollection is correct, I believe the resolution was moved by the late Right Hon. W. L. Mackenzie King. No action was ever taken by successive Liberal governments to implement that commitment in the 36 years between 1921 and 1957. Liberal governments were in office for 31 of those 36 years, and they left office in 1957 without having implemented one iota of a comprehensive health insurance program.
At the end of the war in 1945 they brought down the excellent green book proposals which contained many fine proposals, among which was comprehensive health insurance. No action was taken. On January 1, 1947, the provincial government of Saskatchewan launched the first comprehensive hospital insurance program not only in Canada

February 2, 1976
Medical Care
but in North America. But where was the Liberal government in Ottawa? It never contributed a dime to that hospital insurance program. As a matter of fact, the Liberal party in the province of Saskatchewan opposed the hospital insurance plan with all the power at its command. On July 1, 1948, the province of British Columbia also introduced hospital insurance and it, too, was left to carry on without any federal participation.
It is true that in 1956 the hon. Paul Martin, who was minister of health in the St. Laurent government, introduced a bill for hospital insurance, but it had a glaring loophole in it. That legislation said that the act would not come into effect unless a majority of the provinces in Canada, representing a majority of the population of Canada, consented. Of course, at that time it was perfectly apparent that both Ontario and Quebec had indicated their opposition to hospital insurance, and in consequence the Liberals left office in 1957 without having contributed in any way to hospital insurance in Saskatchewan or British Columbia and had made no move to assist any other province which might have wanted to set up a hospital insurance program.
The government of the right hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker) in 1958 removed the loophole which had been placed there by the St. Laurent administration, with the result that Saskatchewan, after financing a program alone for IIV2 years, and British Columbia after financing their program alone for 10 years, were eligible for financial assistance from the federal government, and other provinces subsequently joined in carrying out the hospital insurance plan. On July 1, 1962, the government of Saskatchewan introduced the first comprehensive medicare program, and again that program was financed entirely out of provincial revenue. The government of the right hon. member for Prince Albert made no financial contribution, but I give him full credit for setting up the royal commission headed by Mr. Justice Emmet Hall who brought down a report in 1964 which, in my opinion, is probably the finest report on comprehensive health insurance that has been written in the English language.
From 1965 to 1968 we had in this country a minority government, and it is noteworthy that the Liberal party is always much more sensitive to public opinion when they are a minority government than when they have a huge majority. In 1968-and I give them full credit for it-the Pearson government brought in a comprehensive medicare program. The man who piloted that legislation through the House as minister of health was the present Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. MacEachen). I am sure he must be very proud of what he did. I would certainly like to hear him take part in this debate and tell us what he thinks about the way in which that plan is now being eroded.
When the federal government brought in medicare and participated in the sharing of costs, of course the province of Saskatchewan became eligible for financial assistance after having financed medicare entirely out of provincial revenue for six years. Of course, other provinces then began to join the plan until eventually all the provinces were covered. But those provinces joined the medicare plan reluctantly, not because they were unwilling to pro-

vide their people with medical services but because they knew, as anyone who had studied the problem knew, that the cost would escalate. There had been a great backlog of people who needed medicare and who required surgical care; consequently, the provinces knew that the costs would rise. But they were induced to enter this expensive new program on the solemn undertaking that the federal government would meet approximately 50 per cent of the total cost. They never dreamed that the day would come, as it has now, when the federal government would pull the rug from under their feet.
For a number of years now, the Liberal government has been seeking to reduce its responsibilities with respect to medicare. For instance, it is noteworthy that since 1968 they have not added one health service to that medicare program, although there is provision in the act for the government, by order in council, to include additional services and enter into agreements with the provinces for that purpose.
It is no secret that members of the cabinet were not enthusiastic at the time about the medicare program, and that ever since they have been seeking ways and means of transferring some of the burden to the provincial governments. For instance, at the federal-provincial health ministers conference in May, 1973, a new formula was suggested which would have limited federal contributions to the increase in the gross national product. Can you imagine anything more ridiculous than tying the federal government's contributions to a health program to the GNP? There is no possible relationship. Had that formula been accepted by the provincial governments, it would have meant that on the basis of 1975, when there was virtually no increase whatsoever in the GNP, the provincial governments would have received no increase in the federal government's contribution despite the fact that the costs in 1975 went up by 16 per cent.
I do not need to tell the House that in September of 1974 the provinces rejected this formula and stressed the need for alternative and lower cost programs which would reduce expenditures for higher-cost programs. At the federal-provincial health ministers conference held in January of 1975, the present Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Lalonde) promised more money for the provinces and agreed to arrange meetings to explore the possibly of reconciling the different points of view between the federal government and the provincial governments. That commitment to arrange discussions was sabotaged by the former minister of finance when he announced his budget last June, and it is very significant that the Minister of National Health and Welfare has consistently refused to convene another federal-provincial conference of health ministers. There was going to be one in the fall, then it was put off until December, then it was put off until January or February. January is gone, and I do not know whether or not it will be held in February.
It is quite apparent the Minister of National Health and Welfare does not want to meet the provinces because the budget of June 23 last was one in which the former minister of finance, unilaterally and arrogantly, made two decisions without any consultation whatsoever with the provincial governments. The first decision was that the federal government gave notice of the termination of the
February 2, 1976

hospital insurance agreement. Last Wednesday, the Minister of National Health and Welfare said that this termination notice was for the purpose of replacing the present agreement with another agreement. That statement will fool nobody. If the present 50 per cent sharing agreement is satisfactory, there is no need to replace it. The real purpose of giving notice of the termination of the hospital insurance agreement is so that the federal government can force the provinces to accept limits upon the financial contributions of the federal government. This is a form of blackmail which will do nothing more nor less than injure future federal-provincial co-operation.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO LIMIT ANNUAL INCREASE IN PER CAPITA COST OF INSURED SERVICES UNDER MEDICAL CARE PLANS
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO LIMIT ANNUAL INCREASE IN PER CAPITA COST OF INSURED SERVICES UNDER MEDICAL CARE PLANS
speechtext:
The
second decision which was made and announced through the budget of last June was that the federal government was going to limit its contribution to any increase in costs of medicare to 13 per cent in the fiscal year 1976-77, to 10.5 per cent in the year 1977-78, and to 8.5 per cent in the fiscal years which follow. That is what the bill we are debating prescribes. The other day the minister said that it could go up to 14.5 per cent in 1976-77, to 12 per cent in 1977-78, and to 10 per cent thereafter, but that is assuming a population increase of 1.5 per cent. In view of the fact that part of the formula is based on per capita per province, of course those figures represent a maximum possibility and not a guarantee to the provinces. It is far more likely that the provinces will be held down to the 13 per cent, 10.5 per cent and 8.5 per cent, with some slight adjustments.
In opening the debate on this bill, the minister said that when the bill goes to the committee of the House he intends to introduce three amendments. The first amendment he will introduce will be to remove the arbitrary ceiling for the years after 1977-78. The press and media reports have mistaken the effect of this proposed amendment. The amendment does not mean there will be no ceilings after those two years. It means that the legislation will give the federal government, and I quote the minister's words-
-authority to set ceilings for subsequent years, in accordance with an appropriate formula to be developed in the meantime, after consulting with the provincial governments.
In other words, after 1977-78 it could be less than 8.5 per cent. It could be anything the federal government chooses to set by order in council. When the minister says "after consultation with the provinces", that is a joke. This is consultation with a club, because the minister and the federal government have the power to set whatever limit they want on their participation and the provinces will have no option but to make petitions and to utter pleas. But the federal government will make the final decision. In other words, what the minister is asking is that this parliament give the federal government the authority to impose any formula it chooses. The government is asking for a blank cheque to reduce its financial commitments, irrespective of the adverse effects on the provincial governments and the sick, and irrespective of the escalating costs of health services at that particular time.
In my opinion, the second amendment proposed by the minister makes good sense. It suggests that where new
Medical Care
services are introduced under medicare, the federal government's share, on a national per capita basis, should be dealt with separately and not lumped with the per cepita cost figures of all medical services. That still does not mean that the federal government will add any new services to the present program. As a matter of fact, it has not added any in the last seven years, and now that it is on this austerity kick based on fighting inflation I think it is fairly safe to assume that this government is not going to add any new health services to the present medicare program.
The third amendment which the minister says he intends to move merely seeks to extend from one year to three years the period during which the federal government will pay 50 per cent of the cost of a newly-insured program. In other words, the government intends to do, with respect to new health services, what it is already trying to accomplish with respect to present health services, namely, to get the provinces into a program on a 50-50 basis and then impose limits on the contributions of the federal government when costs are most likely to rise.
I ask, would any hon. members of this House, if they were provincial premiers, be prepared to launch denticare, pharmacare or home nursing programs, knowing that after three years the contribution from Ottawa would depend on the whim of the Minister of National Health and Welfare and the whim of the Minister of Finance. When one looks at their record, it is predictable that most of the provinces will be inclined to take the position of "once bitten, twice shy."
What reasons has the minister given for introducing this legislation imposing limits on any increase in the contribution of the federal government? The minister admits that although costs have risen for health services, as has the cost of everything else that we buy; nevertheless, our total health expenditures, as a percentage of our gross national product, have actually declined. The only reason given for this legislation was given by the minister as reported at page 1408 of Hansard. He said:
The ceilings will provide an incentive to exercise appropriate cost control over medicare costs, for example, by encouraging prudent use by both providers and recipients of services, and by introducing lower cost alternatives to high cost services, wherever feasible.
I draw the attention of the House to the fact that there is no guarantee the federal government will share in the cost of any lower-cost services in order to reduce the cost of higher-cost services. It always seems strange to me that the Minister of National Health and Welfare and the Minister of Finance (Mr. Macdonald) have never understood that the provinces are more anxious to keep down the cost of hospital insurance and medical care than the federal government is, because the provincial governments have to be more anxious to keep down costs than the federal government does. Every provincial government has had to wrestle with the problem of rising health costs ever since this program was implemented, because for them the cost of health services, in the main, represents a larger percentage of their budget than it does of the budget of the federal government.
The real reason for the escalating costs of health care is not that the provinces have been imprudent and wasteful. The real reason for the escalating cost of health care is the

February 2, 1976
Medical Care
failure to recognize that removing the financial burden from the patient was only the first phase in implementing a medicare program.
Those of us who had anything to do with introducing medicare always told the public and those who supplied the health services that phase II must inevitably follow phase I if we were going to control health care costs. This second phase of a properly constituted health insurance program is to alter the delivery system. The federal government has done absolutely nothing about this. Hospital costs could be reduced by assisting the provinces to institute extended care units for the chronically ill who are occupying too large a percentage of beds in acute care and active treatment hospitals. Home nursing programs would enable many patients to be cared for at home. Rehabilitation centres would provide physiotherapy and psychotherapy for many people on an out-patient basis if properly organized.
In the same way, medical costs could be reduced if financial inducements were available for the establishment of community health clinics which place the emphasis on preventive medicine. Denticare programs, particularly for children, would pay dividends in the years ahead. Pharmacare would help reduce the cost of drugs and enable many people to cope with minor ailments which, if neglected, could result in heavy medical expenditures.
The Minister of National Health and Welfare and his department have never effectively faced up to providing lower cost alternatives or encouraging the practice of preventive medicine as insured services under the medicare program. Some provinces have tackled these problems but have received no federal assistance. The result is that provincial governments in total, as I said previously, are spending in this fiscal year $1.5 billion. For the next fiscal year the estimate is $1.9 billion, plus $800 million additional per year up to 1980. That is a tremendous burden for provincial governments to carry. After more than four years in his present office, this minister has been derelict in his duty and now wants to blame the provinces for his negligence.
Of course we want to control expenditures. Of course we cannot allow health care costs to run away, as they can easily, but I suggest the minister is starting at the wrong end of the spectrum. If the minister wants to curtail costs, he should work with the provinces in providing lower-cost service to replace the high-cost services which are resulting in these escalating costs all across Canada. Mr. Speaker, I think we have to ask ourselves one very serious question. If this legislation becomes law-and I hope it will not-and if it saves the federal government some money because it reduces the contribution the federal government will make to medicare, who is going to pay the costs of this iniquitous piece of legislation?
If, in the next few years, the cost of providing medical services in this country rises more rapidly than the limits contained in the bill now before us, the provinces will have very serious budgetary problems. They will find that instead of getting 50 per cent of their costs from the federal government, they may be paying a larger share than the 50 per cent they have been paying up until now.

What options will be open to the provincial governments in that situation? They have several options. The first is that they can raise provincial taxes to make up for the loss of any revenue from the federal government. Their tax field has limits, however. They can raise the sales tax, for instance, but in many provinces the sales tax is now so high that any increase would be counterproductive. They could put a tax on land, but if they did that they would be interfering with almost the only source of revenue that the municipalities have. They could impose a per capita medicare tax and levy upon every family a certain amount of money in order to provide health services for members of the family. Surely that is a regressive tax. It has no relation whatsoever to ability to pay. We do not want to go back to a per capita tax in this country.
What other options do the provincial governments have? As has been suggested in some quarters, they could impose a deterrent fee; they could require that every person going to see the doctor would pay $5, and $10 in the case of a house call. They could provide that those who must undergo surgery pay the first $50 or $100. They could require each person to pay a certain amount for X-rays and laboratory tests. It is true that for those on middle and upper incomes this might not be a great burden, but for those on lower incomes and on fixed incomes, those with prolonged or protracted illnesses, it could be a disaster. Do we want to help the federal government save money by instituting what virtually will be a tax on the sick? Are the people who are to bear the burden of the federal government's austerity program to be those who are lying flat of their backs through illness or going into surgery?
What other alternatives do the provincial governments have? It should also be remembered that for the less affluent provinces there may be no alternative but to reduce the fees paid to medical practitioners. That could result in a migration of health personnel from the less affluent provinces to the more affluent provinces, with the result that those in the poorer provinces of Canada would have substandard medical care.
When I look back over the years to the Rowell-Sirois report-of which I think all Canadians were very proud; it was a watershed of federal-provincial relations in this country-the report said we must set as our first goal the day when every Canadian, from the Atlantic to the Pacific, no matter where they lived, no matter what their income, no matter what their situation, would be entitled to the same standard of health, education and social security as any other Canadian. That goal will not be reached if this legislation is passed, Mr. Speaker; on the contrary, we are taking a backward step. It may mean that some of the provinces, of necessity, will have to accept lower standards of medicare because of the legislation now before us.
This government is on an austerity kick; it is deciding to cut down on its expenditures, and with some of those reductions I have no quarrel. They decided to discontinue Information Canada; they are going to put a sign in the window, "Open by mistake". I have no quarrel with that, but what are the things they are cutting? They propose to eliminate some of the community programs carried on by the CYC. They have decided not to continue with the indexing of family allowances, and now they are to limit their contributions to medical care. This government seems
February 2, 1976

to have adopted the well known law of the sea-women and children first.
I say, in conclusion, that this legislation ought to be defeated. Some of us will do all we can to defeat it, but we cannot defeat it by ourselves. I appeal to members on the government side of the House to oppose this legislation. If they cannot summon the courage to defeat it, they can at least ask for the legislation to be deferred.

speechtext: Forever!

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO LIMIT ANNUAL INCREASE IN PER CAPITA COST OF INSURED SERVICES UNDER MEDICAL CARE PLANS
speechtext:
It
should be deferred until the federal and provincial ministers of health meet to see if this problem can jointly be worked out. Possibly there is a compromise under which it can be worked out. I think the provinces might accept some limitation if the federal government were to say, "We are prepared to share with you the cost of all programs which provincial governments have financed entirely on their own," and if the federal government were prepared to guarantee the provinces that in the case of lower-cost programs which are introduced to help reduce higher-cost programs, the federal government was prepared to pay at the beginning of the fiscal year up to 50 per cent of the cost.
If the federal government is not prepared to do that, then I say this legislation ought to be resisted. Those of us who hold strong beliefs on this subject will do everything we can to delay it at least until the people of Canada become aware that the health program of this country is being sabotaged. I think that when the Canadian people become aware, there will be such an outcry that this heartless, iniquitous legislation will never be passed.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO LIMIT ANNUAL INCREASE IN PER CAPITA COST OF INSURED SERVICES UNDER MEDICAL CARE PLANS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in speaking to Bill C-68, an act to amend the Medical Care Act, I begin by restating a truth which this act recognizes but which has for long been dismissed by politicians and proponents of government health care. This truism was stated succinctly by Mr. Enoch Powell when he was minister of health in the Conservative government in England in the 1950s. He said that health care must always be rationed; if it is not rationed by the patient's pocket-book, it has to be rationed by the entrance into the health care system, namely, at the doctor's office or at the hospital door. In effect, this bill represents the first, timid beginnings of our recognition that the economy will not support unlimited health care programs.
Politicians often thought that the advent of federal-provincial programs for hospital and medical care suddenly extended the life expectancy of Canadians, or suddenly improved the health of Canadians and relieved overnight their terrible suffering from disease. This, I submit, is doubtful. The proponents of medical care felt that it would improve health so much that illness would vanish. Unfortunately, the opposite is true. The British felt that their health care system would improve health in this way. Some British health researchers thought that health care would so improve health that many hospitals would not need to be opened. Of course, if you improve a person's health in his younger years, he will live longer. Nevertheless, eventually, in the latter part of his life, he or she will
Medical Care
suffer from some chronic illness and take up space in hospital or occupy a nursing care bed.
Prior to the introduction of the federal-provincial medical care system between 75 per cent and 80 per cent of our people were covered by private health care plans. Many of these plans were so good that when medicare came in some people opted to remain out, for their own personal benefit. Thus, there existed health plans for individuals under which they could obtain medical care. At present, much of our medical care is of lower quality than was available in pre-plan days. Hospital beds are not readily available now, whereas previously they always were available, even if one had to be admitted as a charity patient. But now there are long lists of patients waiting for admission. Often, by the time patients are admitted the need for admission has gone or the value of admission has declined. Indeed, the pressure to keep patients in hospitals, a pressure exerted on individual physicians, is so great that often, even though a physician would like to admit a patient who exhibits slight symptoms but is suspected of suffering from a serious illness, the physician does not do it because he is afraid the hospital will impose disciplinary action and reduce his hospital privileges.
Of course, one must always choose and judge: do you admit an elderly person, severely ill and in a terminal state, or do you fill the bed with a young person who needs an operation or whose illness might not be life-taking but for whom hospital treatment immediately will result in improved health in the years ahead? These facets of medical care and hospital function have never been properly assessed by politicians when setting up health care programs.
Perhaps it is difficult for one to criticize and be objective about "motherhood" issues such as taking care of the ill, and the health of the population. I say this because the study of health cannot be strictly defined. From the day we are born, until the day we die, we are never completely healthy nor completely ill. Always, in some measure, we are in some in between state. Governments and ministers of health like to reel off statistics dear to the hearts of bureaucrats. The minister did this in his speech which opened the debate on this bill. He suggested, for instance, that there is no upper limit to the insured services which people may receive. I suggest that is not correct. I mentioned a few limits just now. Also, hospital lists are so long that for practical purposes admission cannot be gained for the condition concerned. Sometimes payments for procedures are so low that some physicians may curtail certain procedures or lessen the amount to be done.
Hospital and medical care programs have been instrumental in introducing some interesting developments. For example, the control of medical care has been taken away from professionals and given to the new super group, hospital administrators and lay people involved in administering the act. Perhaps this is necessary, because someone must spend the money which governments allocate. But the result has been a curious change in general medical care, particularly within hospitals. Before the government passed the hospital program, most people working in a hospital were directly involved with the medical care of patients. After the hospital program was adopted, the number of people caring directly for patients did not
21 130-45

February 2, 1976

increase greatly; on the other hand, hospitals are now alive with the many people codifying, supervising and cataloguing the daily work of the hospital. The reason, partly, is the attempt of Canadian hospitals to reach accreditation standard.
Hospital boards and administrators tend to downgrade the care of patients and to concentrate on the documentation necessary to have the hospital accredited. No criticism will be made of a hospital if patients expire on its doorstep, but the hospital could be severely reprimanded for not having its documentation up to standard. Perhaps hospital accreditation in Canada improved health care a little and documentation a lot, but it increased enormously the cost, and most of that cost went into non-patient services. It has been said that the programs are completely portable. Certainly, as far as physicians are concerned it is always difficult to get paid from the plans of provinces other than the one in which they are practising.
The minister has suggested that a measure of what has been achieved by these health programs is indicated by the maternal mortality and infant mortality rate. I would suggest that the programs have had very little effect on these indices. The drop in the birth rate, whereby a mother is having only two or three children, is the reason that statistics will always be better. Furthermore, transportation has played a considerable part in allowing individuals to seek better medical care. One of the interesting developments of present hospital and medical care plans is exclusion from the decision-making process of the bureaucratic system of hospital and medical administration. In the province of Manitoba, for instance, the minister of health has indicated that he alone will decide what an individual physician is worth, and he alone will decide the value of new procedures and changes that might occur from time to time in the fees schedule. At the hospital level it is difficult to have new drugs introduced or to have new instruments purchased. Preoccupied, as they are, with the day to day running of hospitals, it is understandable that administrators do not want to introduce new drugs, new techniques, and so on, some of which may not be very useful.
A few years ago a drug act was introduced. It was to reduce the cost of drugs. The cost has been reduced to some extent. What is notable is that newer drugs coming on the market in the United States, the United Kingdom and Europe are not being distributed in Canada. The drug act discourages the marketing of new drugs that would be useful in this country. Most drugs are formulated and researched abroad.
Mr. Speaker, it is a great tragedy that when the medical and hospital care programs were introduced, the form they assumed was cost-sharing. The federal government seemed reluctant to trust the provincial governments to bring forward a scheme to upgrade the many programs that were already in effect. This seemed to be in the mistaken belief that many provincial governments would not have spent the money wisely and would have used it on other ventures. The 50-50 cost-sharing proposal has meant the establishment of the most expensive form of medical care. A province that tried to be careful was penalized, and the citizens deprived, because the program was geared to the

most expensive provincial medical plan. For example, the hospital that introduced a $1 or $2 deterrent fee, as many did, found that when working out the formula, because of the $2 the patient had paid, the federal government paid $1 less.
From the beginning these should not have been cost-shared programs; they should have been transfer payments, without strings, so that the provinces could have instituted and brought forward their own plans. There is nothing sacred about having a uniform plan across this country. Indeed, with our regionalism we obviously cannot have the same level of care in any two provinces. This new act by the government is obviously an attempt to return fiscal responsibility to the provincial governments. This, I think, is a good idea if satisfactory cost-sharing arrangements are worked out with each province. My opinion has been that the proposals given to the provinces were generally highly unacceptable and that until further encouragement is given to the provinces in the way of proposals, difficulties will remain.
The minister spoke of the number of physicians in Canada. I agree with him to a considerable extent that the number of physicians is adequate and in some cases more than adequate. Under the fee-for-service basis of practice where the medical plan pays, there is a tendency to manufacture patients. Studies carried out by the medical care groups seem to indicate that there are enough physicians, although there is widespread suggestion that they are poorly distributed. The distribution is perhaps not as bad as has been suggested. For instance, a neurosurgeon may need 200,000 people to provide him with enough patients to exercise his skill. Therefore, it would be hardly practical for him to set up in northern Manitoba or in northern Ontario. Transportation has made people able to take advantage of medical skills available far removed from their home. Indeed, if people are really ill or feel that they could have a serious problem, they often make a trip to a large centre where there are numbers of specialists available for their immediate problem. This is, on the whole, quite a good thing.
Canada has been accused of importing many thousands of trained personnel, especially medical, from the developing countries. Many of these come through the United Kingdom which, in order to fill up with cheap doctors the lower echelons of the hospital services in that country, admitted thousands of third world doctors. Many of the displaced United Kingdom doctors immigrated to Canada and, of course, to other parts of the world. More doctors stayed in Canada because remuneration increased due to our affluent society and the discouragement of the immigration of physicians to the United States because of the Viet Nam war.
My understanding is that opportunities and conditions in the United States are once again increasing. Nevertheless, with a population growth decelerating there would seem to be adequate numbers of physicians being trained in Canada for our needs. Medical colleges are full, and they will likely remain so until the university population drops to coincide with the birth rate. For medical colleges, this could well come in 1984, because by 1964 the number of births had dropped drastically. It is interesting to compare this with the fact that in 1956 the medical colleges in
February 2, 1976

Canada were hardly half full because there were so few applicants. This coincides with the 1936 birth rate, the lowest of the depression.
Governments should study carefully the effect of immigration of physicians on the total health care program. There is little point in having immigrated physicians to excess. There is little to be gained by overservicing, but I admit it is very difficult to determine when there is adequate health care. It is difficult to foresee what would be totally best for health care. I believe that the one group on which forward progress in health care largely depends has been shunted aside to some extent and left out of the decision-making process-and that is the physicians. After all, the physician has had, and will probably continue to have, an important place in the health care delivery system. On his opinions rest, and will probably continue to rest, the over-all responsibility for much medical and hospital care. He usually initiates the patient into the system by examining him, prescribing drugs and admitting him to hospital. In this role, the present medical care system has probably not materially changed.
It is significant that the cost of physicians' services has not escalated as rapidly as in other parts of the health service. In fact, most increases have come about, so far as medical care is concerned, because of the relative increase in the numbers of physicians as compared to the general population. With medical care in place for the past seven years, some fees are now getting out of line and physicians at times are arranging their practices to seek the fee schedule that will best serve their needs. There is a tendency to reduce the number of procedurfes carried out and to increase the number of consultations. It is time physicians recognized that the medical care system is becoming rigid, detrimental to good medical care and, hence, to patients.
One suggestion I would like to make in this regard is that to a certain extent physicians should opt out of the medical care plan. This would increase the flexibility of the medical care plan and would chart new courses in health care. In my own province of Manitoba, the doctors who are members of the Manitoba Medical Association are in dispute with the government over the fee increase to which they should be entitled. Under the Anti-Inflation Board guidelines the minister of health says the increase should be no greater than $2,400, whereas the physicians are arguing that the average should be no more than $2,400.
I agree with what the minister of health in the province of Manitoba, Mr. Desjardins, has said, namely, that physicians should opt out of the medical care plan. Their patients would pay through the paying agencies the same rate of fees that the physicians had under the plan. In my opinion, this is one of the better ways of controlling fees and it also acts as a safety valve on the care of patients. In my opinion, approximately 25 per cent of the physicians should be outside the plan. If being outside the plan increases physicians' collection costs, then they will have to work for less, or charge more. If he can still keep his office filled and his income still reaches the desired level, it means there is a need for further physicians in the area and that people are willing to pay extra for extra service.
Medical Care
In addition, the physician is able to practise a much better brand of medicine. However, if too many physicians are outside the plan, in effect this means that the payments are too low. It is always easy, under a medical care plan, to keep patients coming into the office. At the moment I think one of the best ways to get an over-all reading of how good a medical care plan is for the population is to ascertain how many physicians are in fact practising outside the plan.
With regard to hospitals, I think the outlook for increasing and improving the standard of hospital care is somewhat bleak. I suggest there will be a steady reduction in the quality of care that is given in hospitals. More and more hospitals will become institutions for those who work in them, with patient care designed for and correlated to the needs of the hospital. Hospitals, by and large, are filled with large numbers of relatively low-paid people. It will be extremely difficult to apply rigid cost rationalization, both for political and practical reasons.
I should like to point out that in the province of Manitoba this year the cost of hospital care is to rise by something like 30 per cent. This is a significant increase and I think is an indication that we are dealing with relatively low wage groups that must receive an increase. It is too bad, as suggested by the previous speaker, that the government has not seen fit to have further consultations with the provinces on this problem.
I sympathize with the aim of the government; I think medical and hospital care must be returned to the provinces. They alone must be responsible for the programs and they must decide how much they have to spend. Obviously, health care must be rationed in some manner since there is not enough money to go around. After all, there can be no end to the good things one can do by way of hospital and medical care. The government's way of going about this has not been a useful exercise. I hope that the minister and the government will reconsider their position before they proceed with this action, in order to see whether something further can be worked out with their counterparts in provincial cabinets.

Mr. Speaker, I am sorry that I am following one of my own colleagues. Surely some member on the government benches would want to defend this bill. Sadly, the bill is the result of a treasury decision, obviously not a decision of the government's health department. As my hon. friend, the hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands (Mr. Douglas), said, the provinces are not all the same. This is what members of parliament must keep repeating and repeating to the government benches. My own province of New Brunswick is only now, I regret to say, in the stage of making large capital expenditures on hospital facilities. We in New Brunswick have lagged well behind other provinces which now have enough hospital beds. We are now making large capital expenditures for extensive facilities which are supported by some community facilities.
Another point I want to make is that the suggestion of the minister that he will move an amendment so that after 1978 we swing free, so to speak, is really a preposterous suggestion, one that gives us no confidence at all. As my own leader said, much as we dislike the formula, we did have something to look at. Under the minister's proposal

we will have nothing to look at except the record of this government, and I must say that does not fill us with very much confidence.
We are really fighting a lost battle today when it comes to a properly funded health service for this country. The minister-who has had, both in the ministry and in senior positions in the public service, a great deal or responsibility in the last few years-would be filled with alarm, I would think, presiding over the winding down of an essential element of the Pearson government's program. Those of us who have been here long enough heard the trumpets blow and witnessed the program start up. We stood to attention, and bulletins were issued. Then a little while later the trumpets are muted, the program is being wound down, and co-operative federalism comes to a jarring halt. I, for one, regret this.
I am opposed to the bill. The bill revokes, unilaterally, co-operative federalism. It buries the concept of sharing and it inters the high hopes of the Pearson years. As a matter of fact, I had to sort of scrape away some of the cobwebs to recall that high-sounding phrase "co-operative federalism". Jets were flying from here to Quebec City and back again, with seatbelts fastened, as well they might have been in view of the doubt that the government of the day could survive. It survived because it pulled out a good slogan and, to the government's credit, a major part of that concept was the Medical Care. The government of that day is entitled to some credit for that; I do not dispute that fact.
I do get alarmed about slogans, that were once so much a part of the government's boast, when they are suddenly put away again because they do not fulfil the present concept of need. It is obviously a treasury need and not a health need, and I regret this. I have said this before; I have never understood why words or concepts like "federalism" need any adjective like "co-operative". After all, federalism is a co-operative concept. However, there are people in the language game who like to add things. We have had an addition to the word "democracy" that intrigues me. We were to have a participatory democracy; although that, too, is being retired. Participatory democracy is now a couple of years old. We find that the word is not a bad one and does not need embellishment. When we embellish words like "federalism" with unnecessary baggage, the words themselves cannot keep up with the concepts that government writers or publicity men usually try to give them. Federalism, after all, is shared power and shared responsibility, and the bill itself is a denigration of the concept of sharing.
Obviously the medicare plan should be rethought in light of today's conditions. This does not mean Canada can walk away from medicare or that Canada can freeze itself into a fixed position unilaterally. It grieves me to see a government which touts itself as being one of co-operation and one of justice withdrawing from this plan in the way it is doing. Obviously, too, individual Canadians have an obligation-many speakers have made this point-in the way we fasten our seatbelts. May I say, parenthetically, that I regret the fact that in this very building, at this moment, people are being asked to sign a petition against the wearing of seatbelts in this province. I think this is not in the best tradition of co-operation. The government of this

province, for good or ill, has a good deal of courage in this issue and I regret that these halls are being used to prepare petitions among the employees of this place against the wearing of seatbelts.
When I was approached, I said I thought it was wrong. I said I had a very personal experience in my own family which demonstrated to me the efficacy of seatbelts. I hope that inquiries can be undertaken and that this petition can be stopped. I am a believer in freedom, but the way to protest the seatbelt legislation is not by scurrying up and down the halls of this building. The wearing of seatbelts is only part of the whole subject. We have a great deal of evidence about the dangers of smoking. I am an offender, being one of the most notorious cadgers of cigarettes since the former leader of the NDP retired. He and I had a contest to see who could cadge the greater number of cigarettes, but I think the Secretary of State comes in a good second in this regard. In any event, we know that smoking is injurious and adds to the costs that are troubling governments both provincial and federal.

Thank you very much. I am touched; I am overwhelmed. I should like to touch for a moment or two on a couple of aspects of the program. First of all, the reaction by the provinces is more than understandable. The provinces were looking for a trumpet from on high, and I suppose trumpets from this government are usually unilateral. The provinces reacted exactly as we would have expected, in a federal system, to any decision which was taken unilaterally. From an over-all perspective, I would like to suggest it is time for federal government initiative in health costs reforms. No responsible member of parliament could ever allow free-wheeling, and any one of us who has a slight knowledge of the provinces' efforts to control health costs know that they are serious in undertaking them. It is not the same thing to have a bill which makes a unilateral decision, dumping the problem onto provinces without offering any compensation or national leadership and direction. Really, what the federal government is doing is walking away from the problem. Furthermore, Bill C-68 deals solely with medical services, an area which has not demonstrated unwieldy cost escalation.
Let me make some suggestions in respect of the official opposition. First, a method of avoiding the arbitrary and rigid nature of the ceilings would be to remove the percentage delimiters from the statutes and implant them, instead, in regulations. We have the statutory instruments committee which could decide whether the regulations were fair, just, and so on. This approach would allow a year-by-year examination and review of the guidelines as set down in the regulations, thereby guaranteeing close federal government monitoring and at the same time meeting conditions necessary to ensure desirable levels of health standards. Second, we should establish a tripartite committee to investigate the fiscal aspects of medical financing. Such a committee could consist of provincial representatives, members of the medical profession and federal officials, and could play an integral role in establishing the very guidelines about which I have spoken.
February 2, 1976

In the area of general health care and hospital care, the federal government should suggest specific proposals to the provinces in order to make the system more cost-effective. Considering that the provinces have a built-in incentive in achieving this end-after all, they are responsible for 50 per cent of the costs-they would undoubtedly be receptive to such an overture. Such an approach could consider the standards of hospital admission, the length of bed occupancy in hospitals, the use of X-ray and laboratory equipment in local clinics and hospitals, and a review of the comprehensive nature of medical and hospital care.
Next, taking the typology provided in "A New Perspective", we should escalate a government program designed to improve lifestyle. The Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), on New Year's Eve spoke about a new economic order and said that we must change our habits. He, himself, in the area of personal care, has been a leader. We must escalate a government program designed to improve lifestyle, environment and human biology, as well as some of the points I made earlier about our way of living which might in themselves result in a decline in medical costs. The document to which I referred, "A New Perspective", suggests that over 60 per cent of all accidents and deaths, for example, in respect of persons between the age of 17 and 35 are related to the automobile.
I should like to make the following suggestions: First, recognizing the importance of financial control of the delivery of health services, I propose a new financial partnership relationship with the provinces in which the responsibility to manage and effectively control these costs would be turned over to the provinces, where it belongs. These costs were alluded to by the Special Joint Committee on the Constitution, chaired by the hon. member for Windsor-Walkerville (Mr. MacGuigan) and Senator Mogat which, incidentally, had some suggestions to make about the national capital commission which seem to have been overlooked by the gallery and other people who think the end of western civilization is about to occur.

I have just fastened my seatbelt. At the same time, the provinces should be asked to allow constructive co-ordinated entry by the Government of Canada into areas of major concern on national health problems. It is really not too much to ask that social aspects of our federalism be very much in the provincial field. I have an idea this really is what Quebec has hoped for and what many other provinces have wanted. One's perception in respect of national goals really, in a curious way, depends on whether one is in or out of office. I notice that in the United States the Democrats are now decentralizers and are busy saying that most things are done better by the states. I wonder what Franklin Delano Roosevelt would think of the new Democratic philosophy. I am sorry about this cynicism, but I ask: are we in, or out?
Second, for the serious Canadian health problems of mental health, drug and alcohol abuse, there should be a working partnership with the provinces and professional agencies. Third, with provincial acceptance and support, the Government of Canada should launch a new, all-

encompassing research program under which biological or medical research, particularly in the areas of cancer and heart disease, will be intensified. May I say I am deeply troubled by the fact that the treasury of this government has really, in effect, frozen-which means diminished-the amount of money spent today for medical research in Canada.
I do not think it is responsible to take a couple of areas in health and spend massive amounts of money there. I think there should be a very large amount of money spent on the whole spectrum of health care. I, for one, believe it is false economy on the part of the government to diminish the amount of money spent on medical care. Fourth, much research must be undertaken in the neglected areas of lifestyle and environmental health which contribute substantially to unacceptable disease levels. I really think governments of Canada, be they provincial or federal, must come to grips with such matters as asbestos poisoning and mercury poisoning.
I think ex post facto solutions on the part of the legislatures really are quite irresponsible. We are waiting-and I am being all-inclusive here-as we did in the 1930s in respect of silicosis in the coal mines. At that time governments waited until circumstances were so horrible that they were forced to act. In respect of mercury poisoning and asbestos fibres, I think the workman and his family are entitled to protection-not some day down the road, but now. I think it is a tragedy so little is being done in this area.
Next, the federal government should develop programs of prevention or education to alter the poor Canadian lifestyle habits which contribute to the evolution of tragic and often fatal disease processes. In some cases, legislative intervention and action are requested and demanded to enhance lifestyle habits: it probably would be well for the hon. member for Fundy-Royal and a couple of other members who might benefit from such institutionalized activity. Sixth, governmental responsibility is supreme in the field of environmental factors affecting health. In any debate on environmental health, specific courses of action have been recommended. A moment ago I alluded to mercury and asbestos. Of course there are other situations which have occurred to us.
Seventh, there should be more participation by Canadian citizens in the future evolution of health policy by making public representation mandatory in the proposed national institutes for mental health, alcohol and drug abuse. Last, I think the whole problem of the way our country responds to aging people borders on scandalous. It is not a very popular topic. Geriatrics, of course, is substantially down the list of priorities. Governments go for more glamorous subjects like cancer and heart disease. I, myself, have been guilty of that in this speech. The fact is there are a good number of unlicensed premises. In an all-encompassing health care plan we must have some responsibility here. I hope this aspect of sensitivity, compassion and fairness to older people will be recognized soon by the levels of government responsible.

Mr. Speaker, since I am intervening in the debate this afternoon, I feel that I myself have now become a health problem. One is very conscious of the aging process, especially when I realize that I was one of the people who voted against the original bill presented some ten years ago by a government which was making all things new, bright and shiny. The hon. member for Fundy Royal (Mr. Fair-weather) referred to those heady days when a whole variety of measures were taken, measures that are now being rethought. At the time, I suppose I thought I would be at least 80 years old, if not 90, before the wheel came full circle and I would find that the descendant of that government and of the same party had abandoned what had been assumed so lightly and taken on so enthusiastically at that time.
I voted against the original medicare bill, not because I was opposed to the principle, the idea of the bill to even out for the poor and the rich the cost of health service in a civilized country. I also know how utterly damaging to the fortunes, not only of individuals but of entire families, a serious medical operation could be in the 1930s or 1940s, and how lives and planned careers would change because the money with which to pay medical bills had to be found somewhere from private sources. I can say that in the knowledge that the good doctor who attended our family at that time was the kind of general practitioner who was beloved and revered because of his devotion to his small community, because of his sympathy for his patients in the areas that he served, and his reluctance to charge anything corresponding to a high fee. But even the minimal fees that he charged could be at that time a fearfully debilitating blow to a family whose income was very low.
I am sure that many people in the communities around Armstrong will join me in paying tribute to doctor Roy Haugen, a small town physician whose story, I am sure, will be told one of these days, and yet the only publication which would carry it at present is Reader's Digest which, if

the government has its way, might well cease to be a publication where Canadians could read the somewhat simple annals of those who have devoted themselves to the selfless service of their fellow men.
I recall very clearly the final, fatal morning when the then minister of national health and welfare, now the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. MacEachen), rushed into the House to make his ultimate statement, rejecting all the protests and representations that were being made by the provinces which, I think, could see a little further into the future than the minister did. He parted the curtains and sailed into the House that morning with all of the hauteur, intelligence and stubborness of a ship of the desert. He launched into a speech in which he rejected any scheme that did not fulfil the four principles of comprehensiveness, universality, administration and portability. Of course, there was a fifth principle in the background that should have been stated at that time, that is, the open-ended nature of the cost which the provinces could see. The federal participation was a promise which, one gathered, would go on and on for ever. We should have been warned at the time, because the government at that time was involved in a very small thing, perhaps, in the ending of perpetual leases that had been undertaken many years before, so we should have realized that their concept of perpetuity amounted to about ten years in time and the 'time of reneging was coming sooner than anyone might have thought.
I am sure we will not have an intervention in this debate-various remarks have been made about members on the other side not intervening-from the Secretary of State for External Affairs; yet I would like to hear him because it would make an interesting coda to the debate that has gone on these last few days. Just a simple expression of regret perhaps would be adequate.
