It calls for something. It struck me, as I listened to the present minister as he spoke at the opening of this debate, that his speech did not make the bill any easier to accept. I almost thought, as I listened to him, that he was about to retract completely and renege on the bill when he spoke about accomplishments in health care. He said:
There have been some dramatic improvements in certain indicators. Our maternal mortality rate dropped from 27 per 100,000 live births in 1968 to 11 in 1973, which is now one of the very lowest in the world. During the same period, our infant mortality rate dropped from 20.8 per 1,000 live births to 15.5, by-passing the United Kingdom, Australia, New Zealand and France in ranking.
One could make the suggestion that he might have included the abortion rate while he was laying down that statistic, because if you read the glowing statistic that he has given us, you find that this nation sounds as if it were a nation which truly cared about births and infants, and about dropping of the mortality rate. What a strange, ironic contradiction that as that statistic is being given we note that in the background there lurks another dark statistic which has some connection with the process of birth, life and death. Of course, the minister referred to the various things that so many Canadians who can recall the 1930s and 1940s know, the terrible problems that were
February 2, 1976

visited on families when a medical bill could ruin the fortunes of a family. All of these things are simple indicators of how terribly difficult it is to go back on a piece of legislation such as medicare.
The reason I voted against it was simply that it failed to consider representations which had been made by the provinces. Failure to consult is here again, and it is as necessary now as it was then. Hindsight is always valuable, but as we look back there is the feeling that if the program had been phased in much more carefully and slowly, it would not have been necessary to retreat from it so rapidly.
I hope some of the things being said in this debate will have some effect on the nation. Others have spoken about the role an individual can play in the whole health process. The self-induced disease is the scandal of our time. Some diseases which arise out of the use of tobacco are emphysema, hardened arteries and heart attacks. All these are terribly costly and debilitating diseases. Medical problems which arise from the use of alcohol are of two kinds. One is the physical kind, cirrhosis of the liver, and other changes in the physical structure of the body. Beyond that there is the terrible toll of road accidents which are directly related to the abuse of alcohol in our society. The casualties and deaths are terrible, but there is a far more awesome statistic which tells of terrible injuries requiring the total resources of medical teams and the best hospitals to rebuild and restructure the results of those accidents.
Besides tobacco and alcohol there is the question of drug abuse. Far be it from me to suggest that just because alcohol is so bad we should then feel free to legalize and endorse a whole new set of health dangers. There is a strange logic which is used very frequently these days by those who argue that alcohol is terrible and we should be much easier on some other things which are around. I cannot quite accept that argument. As a schoolteacher, I watched too many students at an early age virtually disintegrate in the prime of life because they had gone into this business of experimenting with all kinds of chemicals and exotic materials. I knew that many of them would spend the rest of their lives in mental institutions, charges against the health system of this country. Even something as simple as being overweight is a problem individuals can tackle.
It seems to me that one of the greatest failures resulting from the approach to medicare used by the government in introducing it was the failure to see the significance of the federal role in medical research. For years, hon. members have been receiving an annual complaint from the medical people of this country that there is not enough money for research facilities, and it seems to me that it never has been more important to direct money and resources into that field than it is at the present time.
As I read articles about some of the things which might be altered if we knew more about them, some ideas occur to me. We hear a great deal these days about proposals for less traumatic birth and for a changed system of birth which would make birth for the infant a far happier and comforting event than it is at the present time. I think there are grounds there for some very careful consider-
Medical Care
ation. If the government was seriously looking to reap large rewards in terms of mental and physical health, that is one matter which could be very closely studied and reported on. There is a tremendous incidence of mental disorder today, and if the fact that birth as it occurs in most Canadian hospitals is a traumatic experience, that the impact could be softened and from that softening there would be a better chance of a happier and healthier child, this should be looked into very carefully.
Another matter which is terribly important is the question of what happens to the child of a mother who smokes heavily, or at all, during the course of pregnancy. It seems that the effects are various. At least one researcher has suggested that the offspring of mothers who smoke during pregnancy will have significantly greater difficulty learning to read and, in a sense, lower intelligence than if the mother had not smoked. If ever there was a matter on which we should zero in, this is it. The expenditure is not entirely medical; it is spread throughout the school system.
A word has come into our language in the past ten years describing a child with reading difficulties, which cannot be understood because the parents are intelligent; there are books in the home and the mother and father read to him: yet the child cannot read. So we have the word dyslexia, which simply means the child cannot read or has trouble reading. It sounds terribly medical and the educational faculty learned long ago to borrow medical or pseudomedical terms to mystify the public about what was really under discussion. Yet there is a tremendous load of expense in the educational institutions of this land, as well as in medical institutions, as a result. The demand now for reading specialists, remedial courses and for other help, is greater than it ever has been. In the 1950s and 1960s, particularly in the field of education, enormous strides were made in the teaching of reading. The texts and the methodology were improved, but that has not paid off, and we wonder why. The suggestion resulting from the research of that one medical man should be considered very carefully, quickly and seriously.
When I started this speech I had words of praise for the medical practitioner. However, I am concerned about one aspect of the medical field and that is the question of the automatic operation. When medicare was being introduced, it was suggested that doctors would leave the country. After medicare came into operation, one thing which occurred to doctors was that the centralized medicare system was a far better bill collector than the private physician had ever been. I know that the good doctor I spoke about earlier would be a far wealthier man now had he been as efficient at collecting as medicare has been. Under medicare, the doctor is always paid, or almost always, for his efforts. From that and a variety of other things has come the automatic operation. The tonsillectomy is perhaps the prime offender, and the hysterectomy comes close to it. Again I will trespass on ground which I expect will be the subject of a later debate, and refer to abortion on demand. That would open an entirely new dimension in the field of the automatic operation.
I would have thought that one of the criteria to distinguish between the physician and the quack was that the former had the professional sense to say no to a patient.

February 2, 1976
Medical Care
That aspect of medicine would be breached in a strange way if the appeal for abortion on demand were granted by this or any other parliament. Perhaps the medical people themselves need to consider very seriously the question of the operation that is so taken for granted that almost anyone who shows up receives it.
Finally, I should like to mention the other serious and disturbing question, that of the artificial prolongation of life itself. This is very important to provinces that obtain a continual inflow of retirees from other parts of the country. It is an important matter in British Columbia. One must be very careful in talking about it because life is sweet still-in spite of the rule of the Liberal government opposite. There is a tendency to cling to life and to hope for a long, happy and useful life.
I am disturbed when I see some of the things that are possible now with modern medical techniques. I know that massive surgery is being and can be carried out on people when the possibility of their living even a year or a year and a half longer is very slender indeed. But the technique is there, the physician is there, the facilities are there, medicare will take care of it, and so the surgery is done. In some cases it seems to me, from my layman's point of view, that the added brief months of life are months of pain and misery and the death that was inevitable is simply slightly postponed. There is no return to a useful, happy or productive life at all. I do not know just how this can or should be approached.
I am afraid nobody believes in an after life any more, least of all some of the churches and some of the preachers. The great Paul Robeson, who died recently, in a song that many people associated with him, "Old Man River," sang the line "We're tired o' living but feared o' dying". I think this describes a large portion of our population at the present time.
In the field of medical research and in an area where institutions can complement each other, I should like to refer to the studies of Dr. Kubler-Ross on death and dying. I know that several churches, the United Church particularly, have held seminars, discussions and classes for ministers so that they could listen to Dr. Kubler-Ross and read her books. I suspect sometimes that her latest writings must be an embarrassment to some of the clergy, because the more she studies the problems of death and dying, the more she has become convinced, not just that there is a hope of an after life but a very good possibility of it. We can take heart to find that concept returning to the churches even by a roundabout route.

There was a poet who said, "Go not gentle into that good night; Rage, rage against the dying of the light." One sees that Dr. Kubler-Ross knows that there is a time when rage, rage against dying is part of the process. One would hope that somehow a certain dignity could be restored to death and that it might be more acceptable than it has been for a very long time in our society. It should not be a grim topic, because the gift of life implies also the gift of death, and were we as a people able to face death then we would have less of a problem with medicare and our governments, federal and provincial, would have less of a problem.

Mr. Speaker, I would ask that the government pay more attention to the provinces this time around than the previous time around. I would plead, again, that the federal government regard funding of medical research in this country as one of the most important and, ultimately, one of the least inflationary places in which they can put their money.

speakeroldname: Mr. Bob Kaplan (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Health and Welfare
subsubtopic: COST OF INSURED SERVICES UNDER MEDICAL CARE PLANS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to apologize to the House and to members of the opposition who have pointed to my absence from the House this afternoon. I have been in and out, doing some telephoning in connection with the event that is keeping the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Lalonde) from the House, that is, the federal-provincial conference of welfare ministers which begins tonight. I regret, and the minister very much regrets, that he cannot be here, but I can assure all hon. members that we look forward to this bill proceeding to committee, at which time all the points raised and the suggestions of the hon. member for Fundy-Royal (Mr. Fairweather) can be gone into.
My observation is that there are so many accusations being made that it is hard to know where to begin. It has
February 2, 1976

always been that way with medicare. It has provoked a lot of charges and criticisms which later turn out to be false. I should like to look at a couple of accusations associated with the history of medicare and show how wrong the opposition has been and how wrong the criticisms of the program have been. It was widely predicted, for example, that Canada would cease to be an attractive country for doctors to practice in once medicare was adopted, that the immigration of doctors from abroad would dry up. It was felt that our doctors would emigrate to other countries in droves, and that medical students would be less interested in going to medical school because the practice of medicine would be so unattractive. This was heard from critics all over the place when medicare was introduced.
What are the facts? The immigration of doctors from abroad has more than doubled. It increased from an average of 600 per year to about 1,400 per year several years after passage of the act. The emigration, or movement of Canadian doctors to other countries, particularly to the United States, has gone away down from previous levels. For the first time ever, the universities of Canada cannot accommodate all of the absolutely first-class students who wished to enroll in medical school. How wrong can critics be?
Another common prediction was that without patient financial participation at the time of or in direct relation to the medical service, doctors would simply be swamped, the public would go wild and the quality of medical care decrease. What happened? When medicare first came in there was some increase in demand for service in most parts of the country, largely because previously uninsured people and those who had inadequate insurance now had the same financial access to health care as the more affluent.
It is impossible to measure the extent to which this took place, because no comparable data exist for the premedicare period. There is no doubt that the magnitude and duration of this increased demand varied inversely with the level of meaningful, pre-existing insurance coverage and also with the previous availability of doctors, as might be expected. The people who needed medical attention began to use the system once we had it. More recent data indicates that utilization rates are levelling off and, in fact, in most provinces the increase in the doctor supply has occurred more rapidly than the increase in the demand of the public for their services. The result is that in many provinces the number of services being rendered per doctor, on average, is going down, not going up. Furthermore, the rate of increase in medical costs since medicare has been rather less than it was for physicians' services prior to medicare. On an annual per capita basis, the rate of increase has been running, on average, almost one-third less than it was in the several years leading up to medicare.
A few weeks ago we were pleased and honoured to have Senator Edward Kennedy visit Canada for a look at this country's medicare system. At every meeting he drew to the attention of the American people, through Canadian journalists, what our system had achieved; the right for all Canadians to have good health care. He pointed out something that amazed Canadians wherever he went; that the
Medical Care
cost of medical health service in the United States, although it is provided by the private sector, whereas ours is provided by the public sector, is greater as a percentage of gross national product than ours. The cost in the United States, as a proportion of gross national product is higher, at 8.3 per cent, whereas in our own country our medical care service accounts for less than 7.5 per cent of gross national product. So, the allegation that making the program available without charge to people would push up demand and push up costs beyond all reason was wrong. That is another example of how wrong critics of a program can be.
Throughout the world there is a tendency for utilization to increase at a modest rate from year to year because of technology, population shifts from rural to urban regions, and so on. We are experiencing that phenomenon in Canada, too; we see, after the first year or two in each province for which we have data to date that the initial spurt, as the poor are brought into the system, definitely levels off and utilization comes down to a relatively predictable rate of increase.
Medical spokesmen had predicted that the financial involvement of the patient at the time of service must be a feature of the program to protect the doctor and the public purse. What happened? Only one provincial medical care insurance plan tried this, Saskatchewan, which imposed a utilization fee on visits to the physician's office from 1968 to 1971. Prior to 1968, Saskatchewan had the lowest rate of cost increase and utilization increase in Canada. After they brought in the utilization fee, they had a drop in utilization the first year, following which utilization began to increase again but at a higher rate than ever before. In other words, there was a rebound phenomenon and for several years they had one of the highest rates of increase in the country.
The medical care program began nearly seven years ago; complete figures are available for the first six of those years. In five of those six years, costs turned out to be lower than estimated, as did the total for the six years.

speechtext: You are not defending this bill, Bob.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Health and Welfare
subsubtopic: COST OF INSURED SERVICES UNDER MEDICAL CARE PLANS
speechtext:
This experience should dispel the nonsense about the impossibility of escalating costs of a universal public program. Finally, it was commonly predicted in certain quarters that government-sponsored medical care insurance would be much more expensive than if health insurance were left to the commercial carriers. Nothing could be further from the truth. In 1972, the private insurance companies in the United States collected $25.7 billion in premiums and paid out only $21 billion of this. In other words, the consumer paid more than 20 per cent above the amount required for benefit payments. On the other hand, in Canada, in 1973, 97.7 cents of every dollar appropriated to medical and hospital care was paid out in benefits. Our state-operated system has been an efficient system.
The Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Stanfield), when criticizing medicare in Canada, stated that the federal government had imposed universal health insurance on the provinces against their will. He admitted that he was not premier of Nova Scotia when hospital insurance came in; possibly that is why he failed to recall that hospital insurance was implemented in Canada under the leadership of
10544

February 2, 1976
Medical Care
the right hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefen-baker). Also, that is probably why he did not recall that the former premier of Ontario, the Hon. Leslie Frost, for one, insisted in 1955 that the subject of health insurance should be considered at the 1955 federal-provincial conference of first ministers. May I quote Mr. Frost's own words, spoken at a preliminary meeting when the agenda was being settled:
It is generally recognized that any health insurance plan of a broad nature should have both federal and provincial participation.
I also remind the Leader of the Opposition that the Medical Care Act was based on the recommendations of the royal commission on health services, the Hall Commission, which also had been established by the right hon. member for Prince Albert. This commission undertook the most detailed analysis ever undertaken of health services in Canada. When the Medical Care Act received third reading, only two members of parliament voted against the legislation. Both were defeated in the next election.
The hon. member stated that when he was provincial premier one of his concerns was that the federal government would pull out after the program had become established. I think that is a most remarkable interpretation of what the government is doing. How can one call this bill a pulling-out by the federal government from medicare? The federal government expects next year to contribute $124 million more toward the cost of provincial medical care plans than it will contribute this year. That represents a big increase in the size of this enormous program. In addition, we expect to be paying an additional $340 million or so toward the cost of provincial hospital plans which, incidentally, include the services of most of the radiologists and pathologists in this country. I cannot understand how members opposite can refer to such a tremendously increased contribution as being a cutback in any way, shape or form. I will come back to that in a moment.
We are accused of not having negotiated with provincial governments. In fact, negotiations regarding the revision of health insurance legislation and cost-sharing have been going on with the provinces more or less continuously since 1970. The provinces have long been aware that the federal government felt it was necessary to put some sort of cap on the open-endedness of our health programs. They were also aware before the 1975 budget that a commitment on their part to restrict higher cost services would be a condition of the federal government's sharing in any additional areas. These negotiations have not produced universal agreement on the continued increase in the medicare program, that is true; however, we must remember that it is very difficult to expect 11 governments to agree as to the specifics of any kind of program of restraint. To claim that we have not had any honest, open negotiation with the provinces is totally unfair.
I mentioned that controlling measures are needed, and controlling measures are being introduced. However, those tremendous increases that I referred to indicate that the proposed ceilings are not out of line with actual experience in recent years. Nor should there be any unfavourable effect on the quality of care provided or the level of coverage enjoyed by the people of Canada.

Some fears have been expressed that the capping of federal contributions will have a relatively greater adverse effect on some provinces. This is not so during the period covered by the definitive ceilings. The capping applies to the national average per capita cost and not to the cost of individual provincial plans. The present characteristics of the Medical Care Act remain; contributions will continue to take into account the varying annual rates of population growth among provinces. The implicit equalization of the national average contribution will continue. The incentive to control costs in each province in order to increase relative federal contributions will remain. The resulting variable rate of federal share in provincial medical care costs will also remain.
Allow me to illustrate. This fiscal year, the national average per capita cost of medical care will be about $74, ranging from a low of about $50 in Newfoundland to a high of $84 in British Columbia. Of this, the federal government pays $37, or half of the national per capita cost. This means that Newfoundland recovers about 74 per cent of its costs from the federal contributions, while British Columbia recovers about 45 per cent of its cost. As a matter of interest, Nova Scotia currently gets about 45 per cent, New Brunswick 74 per cent, and Prince Edward Island 67 per cent. In 1976-77, the proposed ceiling will raise the per capita contributions by 13 per cent, from $37.50 to over $42. Next year, the range of provincial recoveries under medicare will again be from a high of around 74 per cent in two provinces to a low of about 44 per cent in the highest-cost province. Without ceilings, the cost-recovery range would be about 1 per cent higher on both ends.
Let me say again, the provinces that keep their costs below the national average, which includes the less affluent provinces, will continue to receive a larger proportional share of their costs than the provinces that are less careful about their costs. True, it all comes from the taxpayer, but the federal share comes from the whole country while the provincial share has to be raised locally.
One of the peculiar features of this debate has been the fact that opposition spokesmen have quoted many arguments which contradict each other. For example, while the hon. member for Athabasca (Mr. Yewchuk) and a number of other spokesmen for his party have pointed out that the costs of the medical care program have not been excessive, and indeed have declined in relation to gross national product, the hon. member for Oxford (Mr. Halliday) claims that the difficulties that led the government to introduce Bill C-68 were predicted by the medical profession and other opponents of the program some ten years ago.
I would challenge the hon. member for Oxford to show evidence that the opponents of universal medicare ever predicted that the costs of the program would be very much in line with estimates, that the doctor supply would increase at almost four times the rate of population growth following the introduction of medicare, or that there would be a need to restrict immigration of physicians from abroad in order to avoid an absolute oversupply despite a very marked expansion in the capacity of our own medical schools.
I must make it quite clear that the need for introducing Bill C-68 was not related to the cost experience of medicare in Canada since its introduction in 1968. Nowhere did the
February 2, 1976

opponents of universal medicare predict the situation of stagflation which exists throughout the world today, even in countries which have not introduced universal health insurance programs. Bill C-68 was only one of a number of very tough federal measures taken in the June, 1975, budget in an effort to deal with a very dangerous economic situation which was by no means limited to the health field alone.
While the provincial governments generally reacted negatively, and some very strongly, to the news of the original Bill C-68, one province in particular seemed to be particularly dismayed. This was Ontario which claimed that it would lose some $200 million in federal sharing over the next few years because of the original Bill C-68. In the Ontario budget which was announced before the antiinflation program, it was estimated that medicare costs would rise in the three fiscal years 1976-77 to 1978-79 by 22.6 per cent, 20.7 per cent and 18.6 per cent respectively. The same province, it must be recalled, had during 1974-75 granted a 50 per cent increase in hospital nurses' salaries and another substantial increase was due to come in 1976.
The Leader of the Opposition and many of his supporters have emphasized his view that the federal action as represented in Bill C-68 was arbitrary and unilateral as well as without justification. Perhaps he is unaware that the minister of health of the province of which he was formally premier has repeatedly indicated at federal-provincial meetings and in discussions with the minister that one of the greatest problems that Nova Scotia has in the health field is caused by the wage, salary and fee settlements arrived at in the province of Ontario which lead to demands by the health workers in Nova Scotia for comparable treatment.
I must point out to the hon. gentleman that the wage and salary settlements in Ontario were taken without consultation either with the so-called federal partner or with other provinces. They were taken without any regard as to the effect that these settlements would have upon the costs of other provinces and the difficulties which those other provinces might experience in matching them. I feel confident that if the hon. gentleman were still premier of the province of Nova Scotia, he would feel very grateful for any measure taken by the federal government which might give pause to provinces such as Ontario before they rushed into fee, salary and wage increases which would increase the pressure on other provincial governments to match.
I might say that I understand that the combination of Bill C-68 and the anti-inflation program has lowered sub-tantially the expectations of the Ontario Medical Association in respect of a fee increase this year and should have some effect upon wage and salary increases in the hospital field in Ontario as well. The hon. member claims that the provinces do not heed any additional incentive to save costs, but I think he would probably agree that some provinces have more incentive to save costs than others, and can find themselves considerably embarrassed by the actions of their fellow provinces.
I want to pause at this time, having replied to the more substantial points raised in criticism of the bill, and I look forward to the bill proceeding from here, perhaps today or
Medical Care
hopefully tomorrow, into committee for consideration in detail.

Mr. Speaker, I want to repeat something I said in my remarks on the budget speech in the debate on July 2, 1975, because I think it is relevant to our thoughts on this bill so far as the Atlantic provinces are concerned. It is also relevant not only to the bill but in the context of the policies already enunciated by the government in other bills that affect the Atlantic region, as well as policies proposed for the future. The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Kaplan) tried to show how favourable this bill might be to the Atlantic region, but I want to put it in the total context of the government's policies as they affect the Atlantic region.
On that occasion of July 2, 1975, I mentioned that what I called, perhaps in too hyperbolic language, the other "economic crime" against the Atlantic region-though I still think there is some justification for such strong language-besides the relatively high increase in unemployment that the Atlantic provinces will get as a result of that budget planning for more national unemployment to fight the cost of living, there is farther down the road-I went on to say, as reported at page 7191 of Hansard for July 2, 1975:
I refer, of course, to the proposed amendments to the Medical Care Act which came into force on July 1, 1968. We know that since then Ottawa has contributed half the national cost of medicare. It now intends to put a sliding ceiling on its contribution by limiting the federal increase, calculated on a per person basis, to 13 per cent next year, 10.5 per cent the following year, and 8.5 per cent in all subsequent years.
The Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Lalonde) has now pulled in the reins a little bit so far as the figure of 8.5 per cent for all subsequent years is concerned, and has stopped at the ceiling of 13 per cent for this year and 10.5 per cent for 1977-78,
During the budget speech I also said that we were concerned about what the government intends to do with our national hospital care plan. I said:

Under the Hospital Insurance and Diagnostic Services Act of 1957, the government has also paid half the national cost of hospital care. The act requires that the federal government give five years' notice before renegotiating its agreements with the provinces. This government gave that notice during budget week. Why? Because it wants to do the same thing as with the Medical Care Act-place a ceiling on its commitment. As well, it announced it will reduce by 35 per cent its payments to the health resource fund.
The parliamentary leader of our party, in the debate on June 25, asked why these measures were being imposed upon the provinces unilaterally. The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Health and Welfare tried today to imply they were not imposed unilaterally because there have been discussions about them with the provinces over the last few years. Although we realize this, and also realize that in a federal state it is very difficult to get a consensus on many policies, the fact is that a substantial number of provincial ministers stated publicly, not privately, that they were imposed by the government unilaterally upon the provinces. I think only one province dissented from that view, or not so much dissented as kept silent, and we can suspect that this was for political reasons.
As our leader pointed out at that time, it will be very difficult for the poorer provinces to cope, even though the parliamentary secretary pointed out today that some of the , measures may not appear to be so bad for the Atlantic region. I remind him-and I underline this-that put in the context of other policies already enacted by the government, as well as proposed policies that affect the Atlantic region, as a total package it will have very severe ramifications for the Atlantic region. I will try to show that, despite what he said, there will be a substantial probability that either the quality of medical care in the Atlantic region is going to be cut or the level of services will have to be cut down.
Alternatively, if we try to meet the increased costs, other necessary services for the people of these provinces will be severely affected, at a time when we are subject to an anti-inflation program which, whether designed to do so or not, will have a severe impact on employment in the Atlantic region. Indeed, the statistics are already coming in. If the parliamentary secretary would care to look at them he will discover that already the anti-inflation policy of the government is doing what we predicted it would in light of historical experience, namely, falling more heavily upon the people of the Atlantic region.
The other day the Newfoundland Premier, I would not want to say caused a near riot because that would be going too far, had to withdraw proposed increases in the cost of electricity in the province because the people of that area were so up in arms about them. Premier Hatfield of New Brunswick announced certain cutbacks on television the other night. The finance minister for Nova Scotia, Mr. Nicholson, also announced cutbacks which, coupled with the government's anti-inflation program, will bring about a 2 to 3 per cent increase in the rate of unemployment in the Atlantic region, in my opinion, over the next two years. Again, we are the ones who are going to feel the brunt of these policies most severely. Regardless of what is said by the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Health and Welfare about negotiations, these unilateral decisions are becoming a detriment within a federal state.

Among the things I am concerned about within the context of total policy, not only this policy which I will return to later, is the question of how this relates to the Atlantic region. I refer again to the anti-inflation policy. Time alone will show, and as mentioned it has begun to show already, not only that the anti-inflation policy will increase unemployment but will increase it most severely in the Atlantic region, and amongst all low income groups across the country. There is no possible way that these low income groups can even come close to anywhere near the minimum allowed under the anti-inflation bill. In regions like the Atlantic provinces they have no marketing power because they are, for the most part, unorganized. Only a small percentage of the Atlantic region as compared to the national average is organized. They have no marketing power when they live in a society which suffers from great unemployment.
The low income groups in unorganized areas must accept what the employers offer. For this reason they are going to fall far behind. For these reasons the people in the Atlantic region and in other low income areas of the country will suffer proportionately more from this anti-inflation policy, and there is no way out for them.
I criticized the last minister of finance and I criticize this minister and the government for emulating United States policy too closely and not looking closely enough at the economic policies of other western world countries such as West Germany, Austria, Sweden, and the Netherlands. Admittedly most western economies are in trouble, but the economies of those countries have kept far ahead of ours in the last five years, particularly with respect to their balance between the rate of unemployment and the rate of inflation. This government and the last minister of finance slavishly followed the dictates of the United States. We have not reached the unemployment rate which exists in the U.S. at the present time, but I predict that as a result of our present policies we will ensure a catching-up to theirs or close to it, this winter.
In addition to the anti-inflation program and the way it falls so much harder on the low-income groups, such as in the Atlantic region, I am concerned also about the effect of the present bill on the same low income group in the Atlantic region, with particular reference to the level of services and the quality of health care our governments will be in a position to offer.
I am also concerned about the changes to the Unemployment Insurance Act and the regressive nature of the premium tax. It will also have an adverse effect on low income regions such as ours. We know that regressive taxes hit the lower income groups proportionately harder than they hit other groups. Again I appeal to some of the more progressive thinkers on the other side. There are not many in the cabinet. There may be a few but they keep themselves well hidden. I have said three or four times in the House of Commons and elsewhere that, if we are going to make this structural change, we must change the regressive tax structure of our country which hurts the working poor and low income groups so severely.
The Minister of National Health and Welfare is meeting today with provincial welfare ministers to see how they can rationalize the welfare system of the country in order
February 2, 1976

to provide a decent guaranteed annual income to the low income and poverty levels in our economy. Here again, I repeat that if we are to effect a reasonable distribution of the wealth we must change our tax structure. While it is important to have a guaranteed annual income, unless we remove regressive taxes from our tax system we will never accomplish that fact of suitable redistribution. Those of you who will be here ten years from now will be facing the same difficulties we now face with respect to the lower income groups unless fundamental changes are made in our tax structure.
Some 20 per cent of the population is receiving about 4 per cent of the gross national product pie. This is the same bad situation that existed back in 1951, when that 20 per cent was receiving 4.4 per cent. I am sure there are people who are getting tired of hearing me and other members in this party repeat the same things over and over again. Those people suggest that we have forgotten about the changes which have been made in favour of the middle income groups. We have not forgotten those things, but we are concerned more about the low income groups.
Although I have little respect for the other place, I have a great deal of respect for some of the individuals who sit there. One of the more eminent ones, among a half a dozen or more, is Senator David Croll. He was appointed by one of the leaders of the party which sits opposite. He was head of the committee which studied poverty in Canada in 1971. Senator Croll said that unless we count down on regressive taxes such as property taxes, excise taxes, sales taxes, and other such taxes, these people will not change their relative position in our economy. He said this will be the case because our progressive income tax system has too many loopholes at the top and does not offset the regressivity of sales taxes and other forms of indirect taxes which fall so heavily on the poor.
Let me also refer to the proposed reduction in oil import subsidies, particularly as such a reduction would affect the Atlantic region. Someone will suggest I am jumping the gun because these reductions have not yet been announced. I have been told by people in Nova Scotia associated with the Liberal government, in relatively important positions, that they are running up against a stone wall in their opposition to this proposed reduction.
We are grateful for the import subsidies we have received along with all those east of the Ottawa Valley line. These import subsidies were designed to make up the difference between the cost of Canadian oil and the cost of imported oil on which we are so dependent. We are now told that by 1980 we will be faced with a fourfold increase in the cost of energy in the Atlantic region, because of the increase in the cost of foreign oil and the reduction in the subsidy. A province like Nova Scotia will be terribly crippled by such an increase unless something is done very quickly. Our industrial capacity in Nova Scotia in relation to that of other provinces in the Atlantic region is more substantial and such an increase in oil cost will have a relatively higher impact.
At the present time our area is faced with extremely high costs of electrical energy, and if the price of power oil is even to double in the next four years we will be in real trouble but the experts at a recent Atlantic Provinces
Medical Care
Economic Council seminar projected a quadrupling of costs. This government can stop that.
Then again we have the reduction in the transportation subsidies that were imposed before Christmas. This will not help the Atlantic region in respect of markets in Central Canada at a time when we have high unemployment because of other government policies. This in fact will increase unemployment.
Finally, I wish to refer to the policy implicit in this legislation before us today. The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. Railton) in this debate on Friday said that in Canada our main unserviced areas so far as medicare is concerned are on the frontiers. On this matter of medicare-and I could include hospital care but I shall not-may I say I come from a frontier area of Canada. In the industrial area of Cape Breton where we find 19 per cent or 20 per cent of the people of Nova Scotia there are not sufficient specialists. In spite of what the parliamentary secretary has said, if our people are to obtain expert treatment they must be placed on a plane in Sydney and flown to Halifax because there are no facilities in our area.
The federal government has not gotten together with the provinces in order to help such areas where there is slow growth, much chronic unemployment, and substantial density of population. It is no good to ask why the people do not leave the area, and sometimes we hear they have done this for years and years. They have gone to Toronto, and before central Canada was developed they went to Boston. They leave every year. However, they cannot all leave. Something must be done not only in the way of providing jobs as I shall be arguing again tonight during the adjournment debate, but also in terms of these services they are not receiving. Therefore I want to remind hon. members that when the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Veterans Affairs talks about frontiers, there are frontiers other than those about which he speaks that are unservices so far as medical services are concerned.
If we talked about dental care I would point out that school nurses in my area tell me that the teeth of many of the children are almost as bad today as they were during the depression. I can tell you, having lived there during the depression, that many of us lost our second teeth between the ages of 12 and 13. That type of thing is occurring there because of the lack of facilities and dentists.
It was interesting to hear the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Health and Welfare talk about how the percentage of medicare costs in Canada was 7.5 per cent of the gross national product.

One of the interesting things is to see how this member's remarks compare with the remarks of the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Veterans Affairs who, on Friday, said that it is quite irresponsible to let total medical care costs absorb more than 6 per cent or 7 per cent of the gross national product which they now absorb. Who gives him the right to say that? If the funds are being spent efficiently and is providing effective

health care to the country, it may be the best expenditure of all; it may be far better than having increased spending for defence and some of the other nonsensical things such as consultants' fees and feasability studies in respect of Mirabel airport the costs of which are shocking to anyone who comes from the Atlantic region where people have to scrape and beg to obtain a few million dollars in order to keep certain programs going.
The parliamentary assistant to the minister of health spoke of the percentage of the gross national product spent in this way being 8.2 per cent in the United States. As I listened to him I said to myself that the hon. member was arguing against his own bill. I asked myself if it is the case that the Americans are spending 8.2 per cent, and Senator Kennedy comes up here to see how well we are doing when we have it down from 7.2 per cent to 6.9 per cent, why is there a necessity for introducing the ceiling?
Again I should like to refer to something the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Veterans Affairs had to say. He said in this respect that one thing which worries doctors in Canada is the role of government in medicine. He went on to say:
Our government has a tendency to point to the improving infant mortality and longevity tables as if it were due to medicare. However, these same improvements are present in the United States, where there is no universal medicare.
He does not agree with the assistant to the Minister of National Health and Welfare that things are done more efficiently through the public sector with regard to medicare. There is a series of articles now running in the New York Times from which he could learn if he read them.
I believe the United States ranks tenth or thirteenth in the world so far as infant mortality is concerned. Despite the well trained doctors and so on, they have a very inefficient way of delivering medical services. Relative to that point, of course, is the whole matter of the role of government today.
We know people are concerned about cutting down government expenditures today. It is the vogue now on the other side of the House. There is much scampering around to do this, because in respect of government expenditures they believe they must show themselves to be very responsible people. We have heard this again and again in the House, and we have read it in the newspapers. No one can argue against the control of government expenditures. But the main thing is not the level of government expenditures. Perhaps in the short run the rate of government expenditures has been a little too high, but the actual problem is in respect of the efficiency of government expenditures and whether there are built-in controls in order to protect the public purse.
One would think that by now the government which has been in power so long, especially in the post-war period, instead of waiting for the Auditor General in 1976 to come along and suggest types of controls to make expenditures more efficient and better suited to the needs of the Canadian people, would have done something about this. May I call it six o'clock, Mr. Speaker.

Mr. Speaker, before the supper adjournment I summarized the ways in which the legislation before us this evening goes back to the June budget, and I described it as seen through the eyes of a member of parliament from the Atlantic provinces. I suggested that although the provinces had been consulted, the ultimate decision was a unilateral one by the federal government. I tried to put this in the context not only of the bill before us but of the policies that have been enunciated by the government.
I suggested that this policy is detrimental to the development of the Atlantic region, and that it is not in the general interest of that area. This policy should be viewed not as a separate policy but in the context of other government policies and in combination with them.
I said that I think I will be proven correct when I say that the anti-inflation proposals of the government are affecting most the lower income groups, and since we in the Atlantic provinces have relatively more people on low incomes, the anti-inflation legislation will result in more unemployment and, what is just as bad, underemployment, which is never shown in official statistics. I went on to refer to the fact that if you take away the cost of living adjustment from the family allowance, as was done by the government before Christmas to meet some of the criticisms that were made regarding overspending in other fields, then it is the people in low income groups who will be hurt relatively more than people with high incomes. The same applies to unemployment insurance. I spoke about the legislation before us today in the context of the other policies I have mentioned, which are regressive and which hurt lower income groups proportionately more.
Everyone knows that if you are making $17,000 per year or $6,000, and if you are paying unemployment insurance premiums, you pay the same amount, and likewise with respect to the proposed reduction of oil import subsidies. The Atlantic region, especially Nova Scotia, is more vulnerable than any other province to the importation of oil, and the Atlantic Provinces Economic Council had a seminar recently in which it was projected that in just four years there will be a quadrupling of prices. I am told by prominent Liberals in Nova Scotia that the federal government is not going to increase the subsidy or hold it at the same level. Again proportionately, we in the Atlantic region will pay a higher cost, a higher penalty, for this national policy. We are used to doing this through tariff policies in the past, which excluded us from the potential Central Canadian market, prevented us from building a manufacturing base in our region, and made us more dependent on transfer payments, unemployment insurance, and all the other things than the rest of Canada.
I said that the reduction of transportation subsidies announced by the government before Christmas was another left hook, as it were, to the ribs or to the underbelly of the Atlantic region. I said that if all this were put into the context of the policy we have before us enunciated in this legislation today, all of these combined with this legislation, which was undertaken unilaterally, that means
February 2, 1976

that the Atlantic provinces will be hurt even more. Despite what the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Health and Welfare said, the quality and level of medical care in the Atlantic region will go down unless there is a change, and we cannot hope for one in this legislation.
I also tried to bring out the contrast between what the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Veterans Affairs said on Friday and what the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Health and Welfare said about this legislation. One was saying that we have a relatively low infant mortality rate, but he said that the same thing is happening in the United States without universal medical care, and that therefore the system under private enterprise in the United States is just as efficient as ours. As hon. members know, 8.3 per cent of the GNP in the United States goes to medical care, while here, as the parliamentary secretary admitted, the figure is only 6.9 per cent. That is a reduction from last year of 7.2 per cent. Before the recess I was asking why it is necessary to impose a ceiling in light of these facts. Talking about this comparison, the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Veterans Affairs said that the private system of the United States as against the public system in Canada, which was inaugurated by the hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands (Mr. Douglas) when he was head of the government in Saskatchewan-and we are glad to see that the federal government picked it up-is more efficient, or just as efficient as our Publicly controlled system.
I wish to make some comments about government expenditures generally, about the efficiency of the public sector as opposed to the private sector, and then to relate it to some of the shortcomings of medical health care in Canada and why I think the government is now anxious to put a ceiling on it. This is very topical, and there is much being written about and discussed with regard to the pros and cons of government expenditures, the level of government expenditures, and the rate of government expenditures. When I have been in the House hon. members opposite have never adequately defended their own federal government's expenditures in the light of the increase in provincial and municipal government expenditures in the 1970's. They have allowed themselves to be clobbered over certain things that were probably outstanding, some of which I mentioned myself. By and large they have never made an adequate defence of the government expenditures which have done so much good in the public sector and have done so much to improve the economy over the last 20 or 25 years.
With regard to medicare I should like to refer to a statement made recently comparing the public sector with the private sector. The statement was made by Professor Jack Weldon of McGill University, a very well respected economist in Canada. I apologize that I cannot put a date on the article, but I read it in the Toronto Star and shoved it into my pocket. Fortunately today I came across it, and it reads as follows:
The government is providing public goods which, if they passed through the market place, would be badly provided.
If the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) had read this article before he gave his speech before the Canadian Club he would have been much more sophisticated in his approach.
Medical Care
There is a whole range of pretensions in our style of living which is going to ensure the growth of government, quite apart from ideology.
Professor Weldon also said:
You can't run a police force through the market system efficiently, or an art gallery; and the roads can't all have tailgates.
The government does things best where one person's actions affect another man. The market is best in many things where it affects you but not the rest of society.
Some of the right wingers in the Tory Party running for leadership should be here to listen to some of this. Professor Weldon talks of education, and he should know because he is involved with education, just as I have been; tye all know it is one of the most subsidized industries in Canada, but that's a healthy thing. Professor Weldon said:
Take education. In an educated society, the education of the individual confers benefits on the whole of society. That is why traditionally one of the first things a developing society does is to provide free education.
Take the field of health. It would be absurd to let the market look after vaccination. The rich people couldn't ensure their health just by having medical services for themselves, because the diseases of the poor wouldn't spare those with money. They have to get rid of the rats and fleas of the poor to spare themselves from bubonic plague.
The real problem isn't so much that government grows: on the contrary that is inevitable, and it's silly to call it bad. The real problem is that the apparatus for controlling the efficiency of government and its ability to make decisions is terribly lacking.
That is the point I was making just before the dinner
recess.
We have a 1900-style government running a 1975-style public sector.
We are probably wasting 30 to 40 per cent of our medical resources because they didn't change the structure of the industry when they introduced medicare.
In closing, Mr. Speaker, I wish to quote Geoffrey Stevens of the Globe and Mail and to remind hon. members opposite of the following:
Yes, medical and hospital insurance are expensive. Yes, there are people who abuse unemployment insurance and health insurance. Yes, it is important to control costs as tightly as possible.
But is the government really controlling costs? Or is it merely shifting the burden-in the case of unemployment insurance, directly to premium-paying workers and their employers; in the case of health insurance, to the provinces. The provinces will do what they can to economize, but in the end they will have to pass the burden on to the public-in the form of inferior health care, higher premiums or deterrent fees.
That is going to happen in the Atlantic region under this legislation.
Liberal governments have given Canada a social welfare system to be proud of.
We on this side and our predecessors were the originators of that, and we are glad Liberal governments copied it. Now the government wants to stop it.
It's been money well spent (says Stevens). Now a Liberal government is trying to limit its liability. It's immoral.
To which I say, appropriately, Amen.

I can see. I only need glasses to read with. I can see through you.
I think it is fair to say that most members of this House agree the government should take action to keep health care costs down to a satisfactory level. When the federal government is dealing with the provinces and discussing legal and binding federal-provincial agreements it should remember that changes in this agreement should be made through a process of negotiation with the provinces. Instead we have had what amounts to a unilateral and arbitrary withdrawal from the commitment made to the provinces-which was against the will of the provinces in the first place.
This was stated very well by the Leader of the Official Opposition in his speech to the House last Friday. He pointed out that the federal government was unilaterally and arbitrarily trying to alter the 50-50 cost-sharing formula set out in the present legislation. He made his point in strong language, and when the Leader of the Official Opposition uses that kind of language I suggest hon. members opposite had better sit up and listen. He is an honest man and does not make such statements without justification. He said that this conduct is shabby and treacherous,

and that the rules of parliament really prevented him from saying what he thought of the minister and his colleagues.
He pointed out that when he was premier of Nova Scotia he was concerned that the federal government would get the program under way, ministers would go around the country pounding their chests, and then later pull out of the program. I have heard this sort of complaint in other provinces at the municipal level. It is one of the specialties of the Liberals to get municipalities and provinces into these programs and then withdraw. As the Leader of the Opposition said, that is precisely what happened.
When the federal government was negotiating health care with the provinces it insisted upon the 50-50 formula if it was going to participate. As the Leader of the opposition said, the federal government imposed this plan on the provinces. He stated that while he was not involved in the negotiation of the plan he knew it was dictated by the government of the day. He said, "Surely treachery is not too strong a word to use", adding that the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Lalonde) had not justified the federal spending limits and they were not related in any way to inflation costs and spending increases.
This ties in with the concern of universities and faculties of medicine involved in research. We are now receiving mail from them, so it looks as if medical research is not a priority of the government. We cannot ignore the letters and statements received from these professional people. I do not think they exaggerate, but state their case very well.
Because the budget of the Medical Research Council is already so small, because it has not kept pace with inflation in the cost of research for some years, and because it supports a very high percentage of all medical research in Canada, the budget freeze will cause inordinate damage to Canadian medicine. Medical research is a prerequisite to good medical teaching and is basic to medical practice and the delivery of health care. The development of young teacher-scientists and of clinicians with skill in investigative medicine must remain a high priority for a government interested in the future welfare of the Canadian people.
Here we have the provinces, doctors, and the faculties of medicine in different universities all in a quandry in regard to cutting off grants to research and different medical plans across the country. Canadian researchers are in general agreement that government spending must be controlled. They do not ask for special treatment, but only that the guidelines of limited increases be applied to extramural research as they are to all government efforts.
The Official Opposition has pointed to a number of areas where excessive government spending can be cut. There was an excellent article in the Financial Post two or three weeks ago which named a dozen government corporations that could be phased out. Another example is Information Canada. It took about four years for the government to waken up and realize that Information Canada was not a priority. Dropping it means a saving of $6 million which is just a drop in the bucket, but when it started out we said that expenditure was unnecessary.
I should like to emphasize the disastrous effects of the freeze in medical research funding. While I fully recognize
February 2, 1976

the need for an aggressive and equitable federal policy of wage and price controls to combat inflation through economic restraints to be borne by all Canadians, I genuinely believe that the recent decision of the federal government to freeze the funding of medical research at the 1975-76 level would result in grave and lasting damage to the research establishments in our medical schools and hospitals. The main source of funding for health research in Canada, which is essential for the welfare of the nation, is the federal government through the Medical Research Council. This funding has amounted to less than $50 million for 1975-76.
In recent years the progressive slowdown in funding, well below the increasing cost of living index, has had a gradual eroding effect on medical research activities, resulting in the phasing out of some programs with a concomitant decrease in the number of clinical research trainees and of employment opportunities for highly qualified research technicians. The recent decision to freeze research budgets for 1976-77, that is, not to provide even a 10 per cent increase which is permissible within the antiinflation guidelines, will result in further elimination of some programs which are vital to the maintenance of our health care standards, in mass lay-offs of specialized technicians who have been trained at great cost to the Canadian taxpayer, and in the migration of some of our best clinical investigators, particularly among the young ones, to the United States.
The parliamentary secretary mentioned the great influx of doctors to Canada; but, as the hon. member for Cape Breton-East Richmond (Mr. Hogan) said, in certain areas of Nova Scotia people cannot get a doctor. We face the same situation in Manitoba. I hear all the time of people being flown into Winnipeg from the north, because there are no doctors up north. I heard this was also the situation in Saskatchewan. There might be an influx of doctors to this country, but in some areas there are no doctors. Although the parliamentary secretary might be correct in saying that there has been an influx of doctors into this country, his statement covers only part of the picture and does not deal with the medical care problems encountered by many Canadians.
It must be emphasized that about 66 per cent of the budget allocated for medical research is used to generate technical jobs and to provide salaries to graduate students and post doctoral trainees. Without a continuous presence of these people there can be no research program. The research capability of a country in any given area of science-like that of any other human activity, including sports and the arts, necessitating the continuous nurturing of certain talents-is not developed overnight. It takes from 12 to 15 years to build up cadres of competent scientists and this can be achieved only in an appropriately developed milieu. By contrast, it takes very little to destroy productive groups of competent research workers and to dismantle the training centres for our future generations of scientists.
I have talked to research people who are very concerned. They train young people, begin a program, and then find that funds are cut off. Some of them are involved with intricate medical research, to do with the liver, heart, and
Medical Care
other organs. They find the cutbacks most distressing as, in most cases, they are making progress. I have spoken to some of them. I say, "Are you watching your budget, and the expenditures of your program in general?" Many tell me that they do not need fancy buildings most governments, including provincial governments, are erecting; they could make do with temporary buildings and do not need the marble Taj Mahals governments like to build. The parliamentary secretary could bring their thinking to the attention of the minister.
The maintenance of our health care industry, which is based on a highly sophisticated technology and comprises all the medical and hospital services, amounts to $2,628 billion for 1975-76. In line with accepted practice for any other efficient industry based on continuous innovation, at least 5 per cent of this amount, $131 million, ought to be provided for research in the health care industry.
While we do not advocate the increase of the research budget from $50 million to this level under today's economic circumstances, we believe that sound business judgment requires that the federal government reconsider its decision to cut back its support of medical research. The infusion of an additional sum of the order of between $5 million and $10 million at this critical time is most essential to prevent some of the research programs from grinding virtually to a standstill in the coming years. I am sure that we could find between $5 million and $10 million in the Department of Public Works. It would mean one less skyscraper going up to house another government department.
I think medical research should be given a far higher priority than some of the programs undertaken by the federal Department of Public Works. An example which comes readily to mind is the Bank of Canada building not far from the House of Commons. The government erected just about the most expensive type of building it was possible to put up. It will cost a fortune to heat and a fortune to cool and, as far as I am concerned, represents a waste of money.
Both parliament and the Canadian public must continue to encourage the efforts of the dedicated and idealistic biomedical scientists and technicians in their attempts to unravel the intricate mechanisms responsible for some of the crippling diseases. Without this knowledge, there is no chance for developing better and more economical treatment. In biomedical research one is confronted with some of the most complex mysteries of nature, and no government committee can provide any lead to follow, much less the answers. For work of this nature we are totally dependent on the insight and imagination of our research workers and young trainees.
I suggest to the parliamentary secretary that we need to do much research in connection with certain operations. For example, it is possible to perform an operation with regard to lung cancer. The operation may be a great success but the patient dies of infection or pneumonia. In Winnipeg a limited amount of research has been done into this problem. Our research people are concerned about such problems. The operations involved are expensive. It takes a tremendous staff to care for an individual who has undergone lung surgery, but patients die of pneumonia or

February 2, 1976
Medical Care
infection. Research in this type of field is of top priority, so far as I am concerned.
It is absolutely essential to the success of our biomedical research that we provide for our brightest young people the appropriate milieu to develop their talents; these are among the best dollars we can spend in terms of the value received. Clearly no investment in research can be expected to yield its full harvest by an on again and off again policy. This sort of policy worries medical people. They begin a program, secure staff, and then discover that funds are to be cut back or cut off. I cannot think of anything more frustrating to those involved in research. Such a policy puts the whole research establishment in a state of chaos and does not allow for long-term planning.
Neither parliament nor the Canadian public can expect to reap the promising harvest of medical research by discouraging potential research workers from entering a research career, when the continuance of research activities by existing medical scientists is being threatened.
Thus there is an urgent need to increase the funding of medical research in order to salvage some of the valuable and essential ongoing research activities. Without these additional funds, projects which are considered worth while by the expert consultants of the Medical Research Council will be terminated before their completion, and many research laboratories will close down entirely.
For the past several years biomedical research in Canada has been operating in an environment of continuous crisis. The crisis results from a level of financial support inadequate to meet rising costs and from the failure of government to realize that research units can remain productive only when investigators are assured of some degree of stable, continuous funding. How can the parliamentary secretary say anything to the contrary? I should like to hear some explanation from him if he thinks he can counter that statement.
The result of inadequate funding on research in Canada have been disastrous: a large percentage of researchers are without funds; most laboratories have been forced to reduce personnel and activity drastically; morale among investigators is being continuously depressed; few young people are choosing research as a career. Efficient research cannot be performed when the availability of an investigator's tools and assistants is being constantly reduced. Indeed most researchers are beginning to wonder whether or not they will have the resources, from one year to the next, to continue in the work for which they have been trained and to which they have dedicated their careers.
Most biomedical research in Canada is supported by the federal government. The current annual budget of the Medical Research Council is less than $50 million, approximately equivalent to the operating budgets of two large metropolitan hospitals. Annual support over the past several years has failed to keep pace with inflation. The result has been a progressive decline in the number of laboratories engaged in research and in the level of research activity by investigators who do have support. And yet the budget for the next fiscal year will be frozen at last year's level, thereby not even approaching the inflationary guidelines recently established by the government.

From a purely practical aspect it should be pointed out that most of these grant funds are used to employ people; individuals who gain skills and competence at a high level. Adequate funding of research could, if nothing else, provide stable, long-term, and more rationally directed employment than do the greater resources available, for example, from certain federal make-work programs.
Medical research should be regarded in the same light as other highly creative fields essential to establishing national identity and fulfillment. Equally important is the fact that the calibre of biomedical research activity inevitably determines the quality of health care. Biomedical research has already contributed much to the betterment of society. From a practical cost-benefit analysis alone, biomedical research is a good investment. In addition to the alleviation of human misery, billions of dollars have been saved over the years in medical services and in earning power of afflicted individuals. Consider only a few of the past accomplishment in areas such as poliomyelitis, tuberculosis, measles and other childhood diseases, Rh disease, viral hepatitis, kidney transplantation, hemophilia, retrolental fibroplasia blindness, Parkinson's disease, the Pap smear, and the identification of many genetic defects.
Our present society has an obligation to provide continuity in the search for knowledge and the fight against disease, because future generations will inherit our failures as well as our achievements.
As I said earlier, I have met with these medical people. I am not just going to take a blanket statement from them that they are spending all their dollars wisely. I put this to them on a number of occasions. They assured me that they are watching their budget and spending their dollars wisely. 1 do not know if the parliamentary secretary has met with any of these little groups in the area of Toronto he represents. If not, I suggest that he meet with some of them, question them, and look at their facilities.
