subsubtopic: COST OF INSURED SERVICES UNDER MEDICAL CARE PLANS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, many members have already spoken. I certainly do not wish to be redundant and cover this bill several times. Most of us agree that through our two major national health schemes we experience comprehensive coverage which is available to everyone in Canada. I do not believe the coverage is an issue, but the cost certainly is.
Hospital costs accelerated 25 per cent in the last fiscal year, and according to estimates will accelerate another 20 per cent during the current fiscal year. I ask the House to consider 45 per cent in two years. In my opinion that is a very large increase, one that we cannot expect to have year by year and keep our budget in reasonable form.
You do not have to be a mathematical genius to comprehend that changes are required to keep these costs from swallowing up our entire federal budget. We must also consider our partners in the provincial form of government because they too cannot afford these accelerating costs.
The question is not whether a change is required, but what form that change will be. The government has proposed ceilings on the rate of growth of the federal per capita medicare contributions over the next few years. The minister has said he will make accommodations over the next two years. The increase for 1976-77 will be 13.5 per cent and, in 1977-78, 10.5 per cent. That will give a breathing period to come to some sort of agreement with the provinces in order that we can have a rational system.
I do not wish to belabour the arguments for or against the proposal of the minister; what I should like to contribute to the debate, if possible, are some positive recommendations, not on how to share health costs with the provinces but on how we may cut down cost not only for the
Medical Care
federal government but for the provinces as well. I think we should zero in on preventive, new methods for getting Canadians to be health conscious at an early age.
I think it is a fair statement that more adult Canadians spend more time on their cars than on their health. I believe that the educational job we are doing in our society on the subject of health and its problems can only be described as second rate. I refer to teaching people about things like drugs, alcoholism, smoking, and the improper use of foods which we know are detrimental to our health.
Let me give the House an example. We all realize that grain is a very nutritious part of our diet. But what do we do with it, Mr. Speaker? We coat it with sugar, advertise it like mad, and end up with a product that is actually detrimental to the health mainly of our children.
The hon. member from Winnipeg who spoke just prior to me talked about scientific research and the need for more money for such research. May I suggest to the House that we have done the scientific research. We know, for example, that sugar in its refined form is detrimental to our health. We do not require any more research on that subject. What we need is to follow up the research we have already done. If we were to do so, I am sure the health of this nation would improve to a very considerable extent.
The key to any new approach to good health in Canada is education, and that education starts, of course, with our children. We have one of the most sophisticated communication networks in the world. Besides television, films, and graphics we have the means to implement a health conscious approach not only in our children but in the whole spectrum of Canadian society.
Yet what are we members of parliament doing in this regard? In this debate we are arguing about how we are going to share health costs. That is the same sort of argument that we had during the inflation debate. When we brought in the anti-inflation board legislation we realized it was not the cure-all but a stop-gap. As with the antiinflation board and the guidelines, what we have to do during the next two or three years is to find some permanent solutions.
I do not feel that we have addressed the problem we are facing in Canada of mounting health costs. It is not a question of how these costs are to be distributed or whether we can carry on for the next 20 or 30 years with escalating costs; it is a question of what we are going to do as Canadians about the various food substances, for example, that contribute to bad health. We know that honey is a much better substitute for sugar. The trouble is, we do absolutely nothing with this information. I believe the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Lalonde) has a very important job to do in making sure that this information is brought to light in its most cogent form. In the same way the provincial governments and, if I may say so, the medical profession and the teachers also have an important role to play.
Being from the province of British Columbia I should now like to touch on a subject very dear to my heart, namely, damage done to our health by drugs such as heroin. We know that heroin is a very dangerous drug, yet all we hear are pious sermons about why we should not take such a drug, about its evils and ravages. What we

February 2, 1976
Medical Care
should do is to get down to the nub of the matter and take people to see drug addicts in hospitals. Are children in their most formative years, children in junior high school or in high school when impressions that are made last a long time, taken to alcoholic or cancer wards to see the ravages of alcohol or smoking? I think that is not the case. Is this too sensitive a subject for these children? Must they only be shown film slides illustrating that drugs, smoking, and so on are bad for health, or should we not be actually bringing them into contact with those people who suffer from the ravages of smoking? I am sure this would be a much more intelligent way of addressing ourselves to the problem.
As I have said, Mr. Speaker, the solution to the problem is education, not only of our younger people, which is where basically we must put our emphasis, but of all segments of our society. I do not think members of parliament are keenly aware of the benefits of exercise and of what lack of exercise does to one's heart. Perhaps I can have the finger pointed at me because this is not one of my strong points. But my point is that we are deviating from the true course by not using the information that we have already obtained. I think it is fruitless to continue more and more scientific research; we must start to apply some of the things we have already learned. Until somebody shows me that we are ready to use the knowledge we already have, I despair at pouring more and more millions of dollars into research.

speechtext: This seems to me to be pouring money down the drain with no return. The hon. member opposite says that is hogwash. The point I want to get across in this debate is that we should put the emphasis where the emphasis should be, not on squabbling between political parties as to where the money should be spent and how it should be shared, each year looking for more and more money to take out of taxpayers' pockets. speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Anderson) a few moments ago called this debate squabbling between political parties.

subsubtopic: COST OF INSURED SERVICES UNDER MEDICAL CARE PLANS
speechtext: I don't know how he would know, but let me say to the hon. member for Comox-Alberni, through you, Mr. Speaker, that there is a greater issue at stake than mere squabbling. In this bill we are debating a fundamental reversal of a policy that was implemented with hope over a number of years by a government headed by a former prime minister, now dead, on the basis that there would be equal supply of medical care to the people of this country, regardless of what area of the country in which they lived.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council
subsubtopic: COST OF INSURED SERVICES UNDER MEDICAL CARE PLANS
speechtext: How has that changed?

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Progressive Conservative Party Deputy House Leader
subsubtopic: COST OF INSURED SERVICES UNDER MEDICAL CARE PLANS
speechtext:
If the hon. member for Nipissing (Mr. Blais) will stay quiet for a minute, or go back to sleep, I will wake him up when I come to that point in my speech. That was a principle of the late Lester B. Pearson, that there would be some measure of equality of medical care across this country.
What we have now in this bill is an arbitrary, unilateral approach to health care in Canada. This is much more than just merely a change of burden in the cost-sharing of medical care across this country, although that is a part of it. What is happening as a result of this bill is a fundamental change in direction. What is happening is that the government unilaterally, without consultation, has decided to make a change in a program which in the first place was urged, cajoled, pushed, and kicked on to the provinces. The provinces, having accepted the program based hopefully on some principle of equity, are now faced with this government pulling the rug from under them and the provincial taxpayers. The government is shifting the burden to those provinces and off its own back, all in the name of restraint.
I begin to wonder sometimes where in the name of restraint the criteria are to be found. What rationale is behind this red-pencilling of projects? This is a very serious thing when it deals with established services of government and what, in the present philosophy of our times, was meant to protect people against those accidents of life over which they have no control. That is the essence of medical care.
Certainly, as the hon. member for Comox-Alberni says, there ought to be some emphasis on preventive measures and there ought to be emphasis on scientific research, but how can the people of this country, and how can the provincial governments, believe the hon. member for Comox-Alberni when he stands behind and supports a Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Lalonde), who has acted in a way described by the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Stanfield) as treacherous as far as the provinces are concerned?
The key is, of course, education in the long run, but we are not talking about just the long run. We are talking about provinces that have built their medical delivery systems on the basis of a program which was urged upon them by the federal government.
The minister says this bill is designed to give some incentive to the lowering of medical care costs. With all respect to the minister, that is pure sophistry. The provinces are striving in any event without this program to lower medical costs. If you go across this country from
February 2, 1976

province to province, what will you see? You will see that the public is in an uproar because governments have decided to close hospitals. You will see the public in an uproar because governments have decided to limit what they have been led to accept in terms of over-all care.
Some provinces are considering pharmacare and have been discussing it, and some provinces are considering dental care and are considering that. They now say no because of the difficulties they face in financing these programs. They cannot go ahead with these things. Even existing facilities and services are being cut.
The provinces need no incentive to restrain costs. That is exactly what they have been doing. What happens as a result of this bill is pure and simply the placing of a ceiling on the federal government's contribution. This is not a ceiling on the cost of delivering medical care to Canadians, it is merely placing a ceiling on the federal government's contribution to it. That is the treachery the Leader of the Opposition spoke about last week.
What the government is doing is placing the great burden of cost on the backs of the sick, who are not voluntarily sick. The government is placing the burden on those people who are least able to afford it. What the government is doing by this unilateral change is placing a heavier and heavier burden on the provinces which are least able to maintain a standard of medical care without a generous federal contribution. Hon. members over there can shake their heads, but that is what the government is doing. I think it is the duty of members in this House, not just those on this side but on the other side as well, not merely to arise and shalom toward the Minister of National Health, but to think about this from the point of view of the costs which the government is shifting to the shoulders of the constituents they represent.
Hon. members opposite have the right to speak in this House, and the right to speak freely, and I hope they will enter this debate in that vein as it continues. I hope they will, as the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) suggests, ask the minister to reconsider the position he has taken in this bill, a position which has been universally condemned by every provincial minister of health in this country except one.
What is the alternative to this situation? There is only so much retrenchment that can occur from the point of view of the delivery of medical services. There is only so much that can be done in terms of cost saving. There can certainly be a lessening of the increase in fees and in the increase in salaries and wages. There are only so many hospitals, clinics, and other facilities which can be closed. There are only so many urgent problems which can be overlooked. Somewhere along the way something has to give.
An hon. member who spoke earlier asked some important questions. He asked what the provinces are supposed to do. Are they supposed to raise sales taxes, or are they supposed to increase land taxes? Is there to be a fee attached for services under this program? Is there to be a return to the iniquitous per capita tax?
In some way or another services in respect of medical care must be provided, at least to a certain level. In some way we have to continue research programs which have been started with so much hope and which will have so
Medical Care
many benefits in the short and in the long run. Certainly the only alternative then to the provinces and, therefore, to the people of the country, is a cutback on medical services, a cutback in the provision of such services, a shifting of some very important plans in terms of improved medical services. What is going to be the result of this?
During the dinner recess I read the speech of the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Kaplan). He mentioned certain myths that he and everyone thought would occur but which had not occurred, including a drying up of the source of doctors. These things did not occur as a result of the implementation of this plan, of that government of Lester B. Pearson. Of course these things did not occur. But they are not in issue. What is in issue is what will be the result of this bill in respect of medical care in Canada.
In his speech the parliamentary secretary spoke in glowing terms of the visit to Canada of that great humanitarian, Senator Edward Kennedy. The Senator said when he was here that we had one of the greatest health delivery systems in the world. He was right, and we did. It is a health care delivery system which has generally been accepted by Canadians as such, and accepted throughout the world as an example, but I wager with the parliamentary secretary that the government House leader and the Minister of National Health and Welfare did not disclose to Senator Edward Kennedy the existence of Bill C-68 on the order paper of the House of Commons. I would wager that, if they had, that great humanitarian would think much differently about the federal government's program which he extolled in such complimentary terms when he was here.
The fact of the matter is that the essence of the delivery system will be fundamentally affected by this bill. How can it be otherwise; how can the government say to the people of Canada and to the provinces of Canada-and particularly the provinces which are doing their best to cut back-that notwithstanding inflation which we cannot control, and notwithstanding the fact that it is realized that in certain areas the government is prepared to compensate for inflation, or is prepared in settlements one way or another to compensate the working people for inflation-how can it in the same breath and perhaps from the other side of its mouth say it is prepared to cut back on medical expenses? That is the inequity in this bill, plus the fact that the rug is pulled out from under the people of Canada.
That is the reason why we in the opposition must use the only weapon we have in this House, which is to expose the government again and again and again for what is is in terms of this kind of program, a government devoted to turning around and cutting down its whole thrust, a government which fails to consult at all and which goes in the face of its co-partners, namely, the provinces, in respect of their wishes, as has been set forth so ably by the hon. member for Athabasca (Mr. Yewchuk) and the Leader of the Opposition.
Treachery is a mild word for what this bill means. When the minister spoke in the debate he made a great play about his concessions. I would not trust the government, in

February 2, 1976
Medical Care
view of this legislation, with any concessions for any period of time. If there is any piece of legislation with which we have dealt in the first session of the Thirtieth Parliament which has indicated the insensitivity of the government better than has this Bill C-68, then I am not sure whether or not I could find it. This is evidence of its insensitivity to a very important government service, a service which at one time was completely paid for either by those who could pay, or by doctors or by other professional people who gave their service. This has been held by us all to be so important that there should be national standards set for it and that it should be paid for out of the national revenue. Now the government has decided to shift the burden.
An hon. member at the beginning of this debating period at eight o'clock said that the government had decided to shift the burden so that it will fall heaviest on those who can least afford it in terms of curtailed service, and to the provinces and parts of Canada which can least afford it in terms of the share of the national wealth of the country.
The matters leading up to this bill are important not only from the point of view of the delivery of service but also are important to the whole question of our confederation. This government has damaged Confederation before, and I suppose it is too much to expect that it will not damage it again.
What do the apologists for this program say? The hon. member for Maisonneuve-Rosemont (Mr. Joyal) on Friday afternoon made a speech in which, as recorded at page 10504 of Hansard for Friday, January 30, he had this to say:
Madam Speaker, when we are talking of consultation, we must not restrict the scope of this term, that is refer to consultation merely in terms of expenditures.
He went on to say:
In the context of the present legislation, the federal government is prepared to meet the costs without saying a word about how they are incurred. The provinces have full discretion to plan the extension of their services and the salary scales of health professionals
That is a cop-out. How can the provinces, in the face of inflation, possibly maintain that level of service heretofore enjoyed even by exercising their greatest power of restraint? The hon. member then said:
It is quite obvious, Madam Speaker, that if all provinces unilaterally establish a fee schedule and decide to plan hospital facilities and to improve medical care-those are objectives shared by each and every province.
Then he implied by that statement and the words that followed that these provinces would go on willy-nilly so long as the federal government was there aiding, adding to the cost of the delivery of service. The history of that is not so. The history of the times in which we live is not so. The provincial governments, to the extent they can, have done their best within the limit of their assets, having regard to the services they render, to cut down on those difficulties.
The third point of the hon. member for Maisonneuve-Rosemont was this:
It is essential, Madam Speaker, that the provinces put their own planning in order, not to prevent them from improving the services they administer to the patients in their own area, but to ensure that the improvement of services will be the same throughout Canada.
That is patent nonsense. There is only one government with a universal influence in this country and that is the

federal government. When the federal government moves to an arbitrary ceiling, as it has in respect of this bill, then that arbitrary ceiling cuts more deeply in the have-not provinces and areas of Canada than in the have provinces and areas of Canada. That is a fact. Again, the hon. member for Maisonneuve-Rosemont said:
Bill C-68 does not seek to prevent provinces from upgrading their services or moving within a planning scale,
Of course it does not seek to do that. I underline the word "seek". However, that is the effect of it nonetheless. This is giving only lip service to what might be considered merely an apology from an apologist for the government.
We have a tremendous challenge in Canada. One of the limitations or challenges in terms of our country insofar as providing services for the citizens is concerned is perhaps the shortsightedness of the government in terms of the way it has planned or prioritized our society. We are now perhaps paying just a little bit for this.
At Christmas and New Year's the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), in his famous epistles at the Chateau Laurier and on CTV in which he discussed this new society, ignoring the different problems of the whole society in which we live, cast the blame on the Canadian public, not thinking that perhaps there might be a modicum of blame to be cast upon his government and its predecessors in terms of the extravagant way in which they managed the affairs of this country. If we are at the point where it is legitimate for the government to renege on a solemn undertaking to the provincial governments with which it is in partnership in Confederation-and I do not believe that time has come at least in terms of medical care-then we have to take a good hard look at whether or not the government of the day is really fit to govern.
It is my respectful submission, Mr. Speaker, to you and members of this House on all sides, that in the area of general health care and hospital care the federal government should put forth specific proposals to the provinces in order to make the systems more cost effective. The provinces have a built-in incentive to achieve this. After all they are responsible for 50 per cent of the total cost of medical care and undoubtedly they would be receptive to such an overture. However, the government is prepared, to the extent of this bill and the ceiling imposed, to cut the provinces adrift rather than help provide a level of medical care.
If such an approach as I suggest were made by the government I think it should consider the standards of hospital admissions, the length of the bed occupancy in hospitals, the use of x-ray and laboratory equipment in clinics and hospitals, and should make an entire review of the comprehensiveness of medical and hospital care. For instance, should cosmetic surgery really be included under medical care?
There are a number of areas in which we might consider improving the delivery of health care service to Canadians. However, one of those is not what we see before us; one of those is not to breach the covenant of Confederation, because that in effect is what is happening with regard to this bill. I hope that those members on the government side who blindly support the government, which has acted in the treacherous way the Leader of the Opposition has
February 2, 1976

described, will give some consideration to the effect of this bill ultimately on health care services in Canada.
The delivery of health care services, the matter of preventive medicine and prevention about which the hon. member for Comox-Alberni spoke, and the other things about which he spoke in terms of achieving all the longterm results in respect of improvements and so on, are matters most subject to the kind of restraints we should deal with in considering, for instance, the erection of the glass structure of the Bank of Canada. It is not just the same as cutting off or extending the period of time in which we would develop Rideau Centre in Ottawa or a new bridge across the Ottawa River. The effects of a cut-back in this kind of a program have far-reaching results perhaps even beyond the measure of us who consider that they are rather profound.
The program initiated by Lester B. Pearson was one designed to give the people of Canada the best medical care delivery system in the world. This government is now tinkering with it after the provinces of Canada, with some reluctance, agreed to go along with it and built their medical care delivery systems on that basis. That is the fundamental effect that this legislation may have upon the people of Canada.
The last member of the New Democratic Party who spoke talked about a shifting of the burden. That is precisely what they are doing. I hope the people of Canada will realize the nature of the act which this parliament is being asked to help perpetrate. I hope the people of Canada will understand why the Official Opposition intends to debate this thing as long as they can. This is why we intend to debate this bill, so that they will understand there are some people in this parliament who do not like this backroom tinkering that is going on with respect to a number of programs, one being this very important program of health delivery.
There may be some members of this House who have forgotten that the medical care program of this country was born out of a desire of Canadian parliamentarians- Liberal, Conservative, New Democratic Party, Social Credit, and perhaps independent-to ensure to all Canadians to the extent possible that they would be guarded against the vicissitudes of life over which they had no control, namely, the breakdown of health, accident and otherwise.
The tinkering that is being done with Bill C-68 in the treacherous manner described by the Leader of the Opposition is not in keeping with the principles of those people who brought this bill into being in the first place. Let us not forget that.

Medical Care
Wrong interpretations are being put on the fact that no one on this side has spoken on medical research, when in reality it is out of order to speak on medical research in this debate, I submit.

subsubtopic: COST OF INSURED SERVICES UNDER MEDICAL CARE PLANS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in taking part in this debate I am happy to relate not only medical research but a lot of other things to the delivery of health care to Canadians. How you can separate it from any other part of medical services is beyond me. I think it is perfectly legitimate to raise it in this debate, and I do not know why the parliamentary secretary is complaining when in fact one of his colleagues raised it in his speech.
The test of any society in the eyes of our contemporaries, and certainly in the eyes of our children and grandchildren, is how well it does in treating its old, its sick, and those who are afflicted in a variety of ways. Surely that is the same kind of reasonable test of how decent, how civilized, how human any given society is at any time in history. This kind of legislation degrades and neglects the kind of test that all of us want to pass in how we treat our sick, our old, our afflicted, and how we deal with one another.
There is nobody in this House, Mr. Speaker, who can carry water for the hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands (Mr. Douglas) when it comes to the issues of medical care and the delivery of health services. That is what a government that is moral and concerned about its people and concerned about a decent and civilized society would do. It would do something about the tax laws.

If they are right, if health costs are spiralling, that is all the more reason to expand the participation of the federal government in our national health services. Need we remind ourselves that by implementing hospital care, medicare, pharma care or what have you, we are acting on principles of Christian morality and putting into every day practice what the man from Nazareth long ago told people to do? We are putting these precepts into practice in everyday life, through our government.
My colleague from Cape Breton Island spoke masterfully on the economics of this program and I have no hesitation in lending my support to what he said. The moral law, the

It would be nice if it said that the people of Canada will bear the cost of those programs on the basis of ability to pay so that those who can afford to pay most will pay most.

ROYAL CANADIAN MOUNTED POLICE-STATUS OF MITCHELL BRONFMAN-POSSIBILITY WRONG INFORMATION SENT TO UNITED STATES OFFICERS CONCERNING MR. BRONFMAN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the matter of the status of Mitchell Bronfman has interested me for many months. The Solicitor General (Mr. Allmand) knows that Mr. Bronfman has been the subject of more than casual concern to the RCMP. I am sure he knows, also, that Mr. Bronfman has been a witness in judicial proceedings involving the investigation of organized crime, and has been very co-operative.
Adjournment Debate
I was very interested to see the Solicitor General (Mr. Allmand) say unequivocally in this House on January 28, and I quote in part from his answer:
-to my knowledge Mr. Bronfman has done nothing illegal.
Now that we have established, apparently conclusively, that Mr. Bronfman has done nothing illegal, to the minister's knowledge, I think it must logically follow that any person or persons who have suffered adverse effects because of association or acquaintanceship with Mr. Bronfman must have done nothing wrong either by virtue of knowing him, having dealings with him, or any other of this type of association. This aspect of the Bronfman matter is one which demands more scrutiny.
In connection with Mr. Bronfman and the way that he was being investigated, I want to place on record another excerpt from the statement of Chief Superintendent J. P. Drapeau, officer in charge, criminal investigation branch, "C" Division, Montreal, a portion of which I have already given to the minister. The statement is in reference to the activities of certain members of the force in relation to Mr. Bronfman. Chief Superintendent Drapeau said in part:
At my meeting with Inspectors Belanger and Rodrigue, I reviewed the information on file regarding Bronfman and told Inspector Belanger there was not very much considering all the verbal information that had been passed on to me by either him or CILO-East and that we should get to work on this immediately with a view to documenting the information and to ensure we had factual information and not just rumours. I also instructed Inspector Belanger that we should make effort through our surveillance unit and our technical services section to develop information against Bronfman and possibly with regard to his alleged continuing association with S/Sgt. McCleery and Sgt. Brunet.
That is all of the statement I will put on the record at this time. What I want to know, and what I will continue to press the minister concerning is the basis on which certain RCMP investigated, and legal officers carried out their investigations, and how they developed information, the logic of their deductions and the inferences which they drew from events, events which in themselves might be interpreted different ways.
I am not an advocate for Mr. Bronfman, but I am very interested in the background and what has gone on. The RCMP is a great police force, but all of its members are not infallible. From time to time one hears of such cases as the Maclnnis matter, the Nova Scotia doctor who is becoming a bit of a cause celebre because of the enthusiasm which certain officers of the RCMP seem to have for this matter.
The Marin commission, a very worthwhile initiative by the minister, should soon be reporting. The reason I mention these two matters, Dr. Maclnnis and the Marin commission, is to illustrate that it is time that more effort was made to open certain investigative practices and internal procedures by the RCMP to the view of parliament and the public where the national interest will not be hurt, and at the same time to make an effort to ensure that members to this force are treated more fairly in so far as RCMP internal administration and discipline are concerned.
Arbitrary treatment by the force of its own members should not be tolerated. Discipline is one thing, but mindless and slavish adherence to dictatorial or coercive regulations, which may not be practical in this day and age, is not

February 2, 1976
Adjournment Debate
in keeping with present day conditions of police or public affairs.
I feel the Solicitor General is concerned about conditions in the force and that he wants to be fair to all concerned. Therefore I hope he will soon be bringing in changes to the RCMP Act and will be reporting to this House on the Marin commission, and will be prepared to answer fully questions I want to ask him about those members of the RCMP who have been associated with persons like Mr. Bronfman and, based on associations such as this, have had their careers affected when perhaps this should not have been done and was not justified. I do not know the full story at this time, but I want to learn more about some of the practices that presently go on in our national police force. I am sure that many members of this House, and the minister, do as well.

speakeroldname: Mr. Hugh Poulin (Parliamentary Secretary to Solicitor General):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Solicitor General of Canada
subtopic: ROYAL CANADIAN MOUNTED POLICE-STATUS OF MITCHELL BRONFMAN-POSSIBILITY WRONG INFORMATION SENT TO UNITED STATES OFFICERS CONCERNING MR. BRONFMAN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Central Nova (Mr. MacKay) has from time to time been described in this House as a most responsible member, yet at this time he is saying that he believes certain further things should be done with respect to what he alleges is a wrong regarding Mr. Mitchell Bronfman. At least, that is what he leaves by way of innuendo. He does not at any time say that Mr. Mitchell Bronfman has been accused of or is guilty of any offence, or indeed has suffered any harassment at the hands of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police. I note, however, that he does indicate that the Royal Canadian Mounted Police office is an honourable force, one that has been a credit to this country, as has every member in his individual capacity. I think that should be underlined, not the innuendo in the hon. member's other statements and remarks.
On January 28 the hon. member for Central Nova asked the Solicitor General (Mr. Allmand) if Mr. Mitchell Bronfman had violated any federal law, and whether the Solicitor General was acquainted with the alleged circumstances under which Mr. Bronfman was persuaded not to institute legal proceedings against certain RCMP personnel. That is the type of innuendo I refer to, Mr. Speaker. There is no indication whatsoever that Mr. Bronfman was ever persuaded not to institute legal proceedings, and if he had any cause of action, I presume he would have had the intelligence to do so.
The Solicitor General has been informed by the RCMP that Mr. Bronfman has, to the best of their knowledge, not committed any criminal act. However, it should be pointed out that this type of information is generally not disclosed in the House. This type of information is usually disclosed before the courts, where an individual is accused, charged, the evidence is adduced, and the accused given every opportunity for full answer and defence.
With respect to the earlier matter of whether Mr. Bronfman was persuaded to drop legal proceedings for defamation-that is, libel-against certain RCMP personnel, the Solicitor General has received no information on this. It might be added that the decision to proceed or not to proceed with an action for defamation or libel, a very serious civil matter, is a matter that would rest entirely with Mr. Bronfman and his counsel. I suggest that the hon. member is well aware of this, and it should not lie in his mouth to make such innuendoes with respect to the Solici-
[Mr. MacKay.1
tor General and the Royal Canadian Mounted Police in this House unless he is prepared to sustain these kinds of innuendoes with facts, and to make the facts known to the House.

subtopic: MANPOWER-MEASURES TO ALLEVIATE UNEMPLOYMENT IN CAPE BRETON
MANPOWER-MEASURES TO ALLEVIATE UNEMPLOYMENT IN CAPE BRETON
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I was pleased to hear on Thursday last the minister of manpower inform the House, in answer to my question on what projects or financial involvement may be forthcoming from the federal government to help alleviate the serious unemployment crisis in the Cape Breton area, that he intended to bring to bear "the whole range of manpower programs". He said that "additional job creation, funding and training has already been discussed and that meetings were taking place in Ottawa with the Department of Regional Economic Expansion and his officials to develop plans and to discuss further with the provincial authorities on this matter".
The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion (Mr. Mclsaac), in answering my supplementary, said that his minister and departmental officials are working with the province of Nova Scotia to fe-examine some of the ongoing agreements there to try to alleviate the problem. He suggested that by the time of the next meeting on February 9 they will have some concrete suggestions to put forward.
A brief profile of the problem is shown in the statistics. Out of a total labour force for industrial Cape Breton of 44,000, there were registered at the Canada Manpower offices at the end of December, 1975, 11,461 people, as compared to 9,810 in November, 1974. The unemployment insurance claimants increased from 8,000 in December of 1974 to 9,000 in December of 1975.
It was because of the large lay-off that was pending at the Nova Scotia government-owned Sydney Steel Corporation, with its attendant employment effects on the service sector of the economy, plus the fact that we were aware that most of the lay-offs in the Sydney steel plant were going to be of a long term nature rather than one of three or four months' duration, that we called for an emergency meeting. We had expected that the lay-offs at the Sydney plant would have been very serious, but we were surprised to find out that the total labour force there would be reduced to 2,882 by the end of February, and would likely go to 2,400 sometime following that. This is the lowest level of employment at that plant in my memory for the postwar period.
When you consider that the average number of employees working at the plant was 4,095 in 1974 and 3,623 in 1975 and again, to repeat, when you consider the employment multiplier effects of these job losses on the other sectors of a narrowly based area economy, then one can easily see that unless short and medium term jobs are put into the area by the government then the unemployment insurance claimants this winter and spring could be projected to be about 11,000.
February 2, 1976

Our hope for the long term is the opening of two coal mines with a coal fired generating plant that has been tentatively agreed upon by the Nova Scotia Power Corporation and the officials of the Cape Breton Development Corporation. Crucial to the whole economy, and indeed to the coal sector, is the whole question of whether we are going to succed through a consortium of private corporations and government agencies in placing a new fully integrated steel mill in the area that would come on stream in the middle of the 1980's with a minimum production of 3 million tons of basic and semi-finished steel. Besides that we have the possibilities of some development arising out of attempts to develop some resource based industries.
The attempt in the past through federal and provincial incentives to attract private industries in that area, especially during the first four years of the existing Cape Breton Development Corporation, was a miserable failure. It is my own opinion that as long as we do not have a fully employed economy operating for at least five years nationally, there is little hope for attracting any private profit industry from outside the area. This, of course, would change if we had a stabilized coal industry and a competitive international steel plant.
One of the things that government has to do in the long run at the federal level is to change its policies of decentralizing government departments and "footloose" institutions of the public sector. In recent years there have been some attempts by the federal government to decentralize other than in the defence sector. I am referring especially to the decentralization of certain DREE activities and to the recent attempts of the Department of Revenue to decentralize data processing facilities in the different regions of Canada. I realize some of the difficulties that are involved. But surely if the attempt to close regional disparity gaps in employment and income is to be taken seriously then the time has come to stop decentralizing from Ottawa only into the metropolitan areas of the country.
Most of the high unemployment slow growth areas that have within their radius 100,000 or more people should receive as government policy first call on these types of jobs as they develop. My reasoning is that the slow growth areas economic base is usually one in which the labor force is engaged primarily in producing for internationally competitive markets, as well as often having a seasonally structured employment base. You will never truly, in my opinion, improve the position of these areas by giving a carrot to private entrepreneurs to go in there; past experience suggests that if you try this route it often leads not only to a misuse of public money but to the lowering or destruction of the morale of the people in these areas, whose hopes get built too high.
During his speech to the Canadian Club the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), after reiterating the obvious, had this to say:
"I would ask private industry whether it is prepared to act voluntarily to distribute economic opportunities more equitably across the nation, through decisions on plant locations"
I think this is kind of naivety on his part, but in any case I would think that it would be much more important to the slow growth and chronic unemployment areas such as I represent to have a policy of decentralizing non-competi-
Adjournment Debate
tive public industries into these areas. Other such areas would include the Gaspe, Northern New Brunswick, the West Coast of Newfoundland, and Northern Ontario.
The metropolitan areas, even in the Atlantic region, are traditionally in the 1970's full employment areas so it makes little sense to me to push them over full employment and let the other areas depend so heavily on unemployment insurance and other government transfer payments. Surely no one in this day and age would consider another alternative of moving large numbers of people out of their natural communities as a solution-in fact it would be a non-solution-to such problems. In the meantime we will be attending the meeting on February 9 hoping that both the provincial and federal governments will have something substantial in the way of projects to alleviate the present crisis. Tonight I am hoping to have some indication of the projects the Department of Manpower proposes for our hard hit area.

speakeroldname: Hon. Robert K. Andras (Minister of Manpower and Immigration):
subtopic: MANPOWER-MEASURES TO ALLEVIATE UNEMPLOYMENT IN CAPE BRETON
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as the House was advised on January 29, I believe, the Department of Manpower and Immigration and myself are very much aware and very much concerned about the distressingly high rate of unemployment on Cape Breton Island, and we are aware that there are pockets on that island which seem to exceed the rate on the island itself. We are trying our best to help alleviate this situation with all applicable manpower programs and services, and we are allocating additional training funds for Cape Breton through the Nova Scotia Manpower Needs Committee. The Local Initiatives Program and the Local Employment Assistance Program have seen about 40 per cent or 50 per cent of their allocation go to Cape Breton.
The federal provincial manpower committee has of course discussed the problem, as the hon. member knows. I think the suggestions he has made in his very thoughtful and brief presentation tonight are very worth-while, and I intend to examine them with my colleague, the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion (Mr. Lessard), during our on-going meetings about this particular problem, to see what we can do. I really wish I had a magic wand with which to try to resolve this in the immediate future.
As the hon. member knows, there is a citizen's committee developed by my department. We are looking for the input of the local people. We are discussing the matter with DREE and will try to have a solution. If I had a magic wand, as I have said, I would wave it and have a solution for tomorrow. We will have to search for a solution and see what we can do about this situation.

subtopic: AGRICULTURE-BEEF-SUGGESTED RESTRICTION OF FOREIGN IMPORTS AND RENEGOTIATION OF UNITED STATES QUOTAS
AGRICULTURE-BEEF-SUGGESTED RESTRICTION OF FOREIGN IMPORTS AND RENEGOTIATION OF UNITED STATES QUOTAS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, last December 18, just before the Christmas recess, I addressed a question to the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) suggesting he might give consideration to supporting the Canadian cattlemen's view that unless some form of voluntary restraint against foreign imports is instituted, or a Canadian meat import law is enacted, we may not have

February 2, 1976
Adjournment Debate
access to the United States market for our Canadian beef and veal. This was suggested the day before the minister went to Washington to confer with U.S. secretary of agriculture, Mr. Butz, on the egg issue and beef and veal quotas.
My suggestion was both kindly and logical in view of the recent strained relationship between our two countries over the cattle and beef trade and quotas in the last year and a half.
I also suggested that if cattle and beef quotas were to be renegotiated, they should be at or near historical trade levels, similar to Canada's five year average pattern, instead of a 12 month August to August quota as used by the U.S.
The minister's response was a very cynical and sarcastic comment that he would do nothing to offend the CCA because they do not want government interference. I suggest, Mr. Speaker, that good, sound, properly negotiated bilateral trade arrangements do not constitute government interference.
Just two days before my question the minister had invited the CCA executive to meet with him and his senior staff to discuss this matter, as well as the current stabilization issue. While I can commend the minister for this action in asking the CCA for comments and advice, I must report that due to the constraints resulting from the Agricultural Outlook Conference which took place at the same time, it was not a fruitful meeting. The minister just did not arrange sufficient time for this special meeting called at his request.
Nevertheless, it is rather interesting to note the developments of the minister's meeting with Mr. Butz as reported in the minister's press release dated December 31. The release announced the end of beef quotas on December 31 by both countries, and reminded us that live cattle quotas had been lifted last August. The statement went on to report:
"During our meeting, Mr. Butz pointed out that the U.S. have a meat import law in their statutes and they must operate under it" Mr. Whelan said.
"Taking that into account, I advised Mr. Butz that Canada would need to provide similar safeguards to protect against any unusual or excessive meat flow into this country.
"We have reached agreement in this context and are very satisfied with the arrangement".
Toward the end of the press release we find the following:
Mr. Whelan also noted the agreement opens the way for discussions with Australia and New Zealand.
"These two countries are significant exporters of beef to Canada. We have already advised both countries that we want to make similar arrangements with them to ensure orderly marketing", Mr. Whelan said.
While the minister did not use the term "Canadian meat import law" his phrase "similar safeguards" does indeed suggest that he was aware of the cattlemen's views, and CCA, I am sure, would like to see this suggestion further developed between Canada and the U.S.A., and between Canada and Australia and New Zealand. I am sure he would like to ensure that never again will we in Canada have to endure a flood of U.S. cattle which collapsed our

markets, such as in the summer of 1973 following the U.S. price control program.
In the cattle industry we in Canada share with the U.S. cattle producers the North American beef market together with Mexico, of course. These three countries are indeed partners in the North American beef economy, but we are not equal partners. With a ten to one ratio of both people and cattle populations as between USA and Canada it is obvious that the U.S. market dominates the north American cattle and beef market, and therefore has much greater capacity either to benefit or damage our Canadian market, and both of these situations have occurred. Let me make it abundantly clear at this point that I fully support the concept that our Canadian cattle industry should continue to be a vital part of the north American cattle market.
Since 1970 our trade balance in both cattle and beef with the USA has deteriorated badly. In dressed beef we slipped from a $39.7 million credit balance in 1970 to a $5.1 million credit balance in 1974. In live cattle we dropped from a credit balance of $58.3 million in 1965 to a deficit of $33.4 million in 1974. The 1975 picture is better with a favourable trade balance for both cattle and beef, thanks to the very heavy export of 100,000 cows to the USA in the last five months of 1975. While our nominal tariffs between our two countries of 1.5 cents a pound for live cattle and 3 cents a pound on beef are the same for both countries, it should be pointed out that when we export cut beef or block ready beef to the U.S. there is a ten per cent ad valorem U.S. duty.
Since the first of this year Canada has reverted to the status of quota free access for beef imports. We are probably the only country with a developed beef industry to offer this unlimited access. The U.S. has its meat import law that can be triggered immediately by presidential action, and while Canada has a very generous access to that market we can never inundate the U.S. market as can happen in the reverse, such as in 1973 in Canada.
I believe very sincerely that Canada needs a beef import law to be implemented only at times when imports greatly exceed the boundaries of normal trade relationships and, most particularly, when such imports are the result of arbitrary forces developing in the U.S. market. I also believe that Canadian beef producers recognize the importance and validity of the concept of a North American beef economy. Yet many of us seem to believe that we can have the best of two worlds, a domestically supported industry and access to the U.S. market. This simply cannot be. If we seek public support for our industry, we will have to employ restrictive import controls, and such controls will prompt retaliation in time.

Mr. Speaker, since this matter was raised by the hon. member on December 18, 1975, the minister has had discussions with this counterpart, U.S. secretary of agriculture, Earl Butz. As a result of his trip to Washington on December 19, Canada and the U.S. agreed to remove the quotas on beef and veal effective December 31, 1975.
February 2, 1976

This agreement goes further than the hon. member suggested, in that it cleared the way for the restoration of normal two way trade in beef and veal. Hon. members will recall that normal trade in live animals was restored by agreement in August of 1975.
Discussions are being held on a continuing basis among officials from Canada, the United States, Australia, and New Zealand in a concerted effort to establish meat import-export agreements which would be acceptable to all parties and which will ensure the orderly functioning of the international beef market. I must advise the hon. member, however, that because these discussions are still proceeding I cannot provide him with specific details, such as quantities involved, at this time.
Recently the hon. member has been raising the issue of Canadian imposition of blue tongue regulations. The minister has assured the House on several occasions, including earlier today, that this disease does not exist in Canada. Discoveries of this disease in recent years have been limited to cattle which were imported from the U.S. In all cases these animals were slaughtered, and all animals which had come into contact with them were texted for
Adjournment Debate
blue tongue. It is gratifying to note that such tests have consistently been negative. I must impress upon the house the importance of maintaining blue tongue free status among our cattle population so that Canada may continue to export cattle to more countries than any other nation in the world.
In his question of December 18 the hon. member raised the issue of egg trade between Canada and the U.S. As 1 am sure all hon. members are now aware, GATT has ruled that Canada has the right under GATT articles to limit egg imports. Nevertheless, Canadian officials are regularly meeting with their U.S. counterparts with the goal of arriving at an agreement which will satisfy both countries. 1.	Two small scale Radiation survey exercises were carried out by the Canadian Army in the Port Hope area in the early 1950s. They involved Number 1 Radiation Detection Unit, located at Kingston, Ont., and were nicknamed Exercise Hope I (19 to 21 November 1951) and Exercise Hope III (17 to 19 November 1953).
2.	Details of the objectives and scope are provided in Attachments 1 and 2 to this document. However in order to put these activities in correct perspective, some background information will be helpful.

3.	In 1950, the Canadian Army was in the process of experimenting with the radiological survey and monitoring procedures which would be required in the event of an atomic war.
4.	The Korean war was in progress at the time, and it will be recalled that there was a school of thought which advocated the use of atomic weapons to bring about a speedy end to the United Nations police action. Thus, although Canada was technically at peace, a Canadian Army Brigade was fighting with the United Nations Forces in Korea, and the possibility of atomic weapons being employed in that conflict could not be ruled out entirely.
5.	Number 1 Radiation Detection Unit was formed in May 1950 to develop radiation survey and monitoring procedures as well as associated soil and water sampling techniques.
6.	To provide the unit with practical experience in the operation of radiation detection instruments in an actual radiation environment, arrangements were made through the National Research Council to utilize the facilities of Eldorado Mining and Refining (1944) Limited in Port Hope, Ont. (Footnote 1). These facilities included the company's refining plant on the waterfront in Port Hope, two of its residue disposal areas (the MONKEY MOUNTAIN Residue Area and the WELCOME Residue Area) and the PIDGEON Hill Storage Site.
Note: 1. This Crown Corporation is now known as Eldorado Nuclear Limited.

7.	Each exercise achieved its desired purpose and provided valuable experience to the officers and men involved in the assessment of radiation hazards which would be encountered in a nuclear war. The techniques devised made a useful contribution to the subsequent development of Army doctrine for nuclear warfare operations and field radiation survey procedures.

8.	A detailed report was furnished to Army Headquarters following each exercise, the content of which centered entirely around the procedures and techniques employed, plus a number of recommendations relating to means of
enhancing the Army's capabilities in radiation survey operations and associated functions.

9.	An article was published in the November 1951 edition of the Canadian Army Journal entitled «Radiation Detection Unit*, which outlined the role and activities of the unit and included a brief description of Exercise HOPE I.

10.	As expected, radioactivity levels encountered in the Eldorado Mining and Refining residue disposal areas were high enough to provide excellent training in the operation of the RDU's very sensitive radiation detection instruments. Some areas of the refining plant itself were also known beforehand to be mildly radioactive, and RDU personnel were invited to conduct a survey of the plant premises to gain additional experience in monitoring buildings and equipment.

11.	Following questions raised in the House of Commons on 28 Jan. 76 concerning the precise nature and purpose of the 1951 and 1953 survey exercises, all relevant reports and documentation were made available for examination by an official of the Atomic Energy Control Board. The official expressed complete satisfaction that the exercises were arranged solely to train military personnel in the use of radiation detection equipment and to test procedures to be followed in the event of a nuclear war.
12.	Further, the examination confirmed that the information arising out of the two exercises did not in any way indicate that the operation by Eldorado Mining and Refining Limited of refinery residue disposal areas located within the town limits posed a hazard to the citizens of Port Hope. Nor did the surveys reveal any radioactively contaminated areas other than those directly involved in the Company's disposal operations.

13.	Exercises HOPE I and HOPE III were conducted by the Canadian Army to provide realistic training for personnel in the operation of radiation detection instruments, in radiation survey procedures and other associated techniques required for military operations under conditions of nuclear war.
14.	The initiative in both instances came from the Canadian Army. The Radiation Detection Unit was not «cal-led-in* to assist in assessing potential radiation hazards to the population of the Town of Port Hope.
15.	As both exercises were very limited in scope and significance, the reports provided to Army Headquarters subsequently received very limited distribution, as they were considered to be of little interest to agencies other than the military staffs directly concerned with developing doctrine, procedures and special equipment requirements which would be necessary in nuclear war.

16.	As expected, relatively high radiation levels were encountered in the residue disposal areas; however no other radioactively contaminated areas were identified other than those directly related to the disposal operations of Eldorado Mining and Refining Limited.

Attachment 1

1.	This exercise took place on 19, 20 and 21 November 1951. It was a very small scale operation involving only three officers and eight men.
2.	The exercise scenario depicted the type of situation which might exist in a Canadian seaport after a nuclear explosion in the harbour area. The Radiation Detection Unit was tasked to carry out a re-entry operation, plotting the radiation levels encountered as survey teams approached the waterfront area.
3.	For this purpose Eldorado Mining and Refining Limited made available a number of relatively harmless radioactive sources which were positioned at predetermined locations along the routes of the survey teams. The survey operations also included the Eldorado plant and premises, as well as the MONKEY MOUNTAIN Disposal Area and PIDGEON HILL Storage Site, where further instrument readings were obtained from the radioactivity present at those locations.
4.	By applying an arbitrary multiplication factor to the readings obtained from their sensitive detection instruments the survey teams were able to represent to some degree the very high radiation levels it was thought would be encountered in an actual wartime situation.
5.	The local populace was informed prior to the start of the exercise that radioactive sources would be positioned at various locations around the town, to avoid any unnecessary public concern.
6.	The exercise report pointed up the need to develop standard procedures for the conduct of radiation survey operations, and highlighted weaknesses in the areas of radio communications, lack of technical facilities to perform on the spot maintenance of radiation detection equipment, the need for suitable maps, and a requirement for specially equipped cross country vehicles to support this type of operation.
Attachment 2

1.	Conducted on 17, 18 and 19 November 1953, Exercise HOPE III was a simple radiation survey exercise carried out entirely within the WELCOME Residue Area, some four miles North West of Port Hope.
2.	This facility offered an area of known radioactivity, and the objective of HOPE III was to refine ground radiation survey procedures, hazard estimation techniques and sample analysis.
3.	Four officers and fifteen men participated. A mobile field laboratory was included to perform soil and water sampling.
4.	The exercise report revealed some deficiencies in equipment and detailed procedures, and recommended the provision of some additional items to improve laboratory analysis techniques, the provision of an air sampling capability, and a number of minor measures to enhance the effectiveness of the unit's operations.
